title: Novel hybrid protein scaffold gap filling using weighted machine learning ensemble, beam search, and mass-constrained reranking
summary: Protein scaffold gap filling is an important computational task in protein sequence reconstruction, where missing amino acid regions must be inferred from incomplete scaffold information. This study proposes a hybrid machine learning and mass constrained reranking framework for protein scaffold gap filling under known-gap-size and known-gapmass settings. Homologous protein sequences from MabCampath, P5A proteoform, and carbonic anhydrase 2 were used to generate masked 11-mer residue-level samples and fullgap evaluation cases. The residue prediction task was formulated as a 20-class amino acid classification problem using first-, middle-, and last-position masking. Multiple classical machine learning models were trained using raw encoded, row-average, and SVD-reduced features, and the strongest models were combined through a validation-accuracy-weighted ensemble. For known-size gap reconstruction, beam search was used to generate complete missing peptide sequences from residue-level probability estimates. For known-mass reconstruction, mass-constrained homologous candidate retrieval was combined with hybrid reranking based on mass validity, homologous frequency, context support, ensemble likelihood, mass error, and length penalty. The proposed framework achieved 95.41% residue-level validation accuracy, 87.50% known-size exact-match accuracy, and 100% top-5 recovery on seven CAH2 known-mass benchmark cases. These results indicate that the proposed framework can effectively reconstruct missing protein regions by integrating local sequence learning, homologous evidence, peptide mass constraints, and biochemical validation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a hybrid machine learning and mass-constrained reranking framework for protein scaffold gap filling, achieving 95.41% residue-level accuracy, 87.50% known-size exact-match accuracy, and 100% top-5 recovery on known-mass benchmark cases.
AI.motivation: Protein scaffold gap filling is a computationally challenging task in protein sequence reconstruction where missing amino acid regions must be inferred from incomplete scaffold information. The authors aim to address this challenge under both known-gap-size and known-gap-mass settings.
AI.method: The framework combines (1) multiple classical ML models (trained on raw encoded, row-average, and SVD-reduced features) assembled via validation-accuracy-weighted ensemble for 20-class amino acid classification, (2) beam search for known-size gap reconstruction, and (3) mass-constrained homologous candidate retrieval with hybrid reranking (mass validity, homologous frequency, context support, ensemble likelihood, mass error, length penalty) for known-mass reconstruction.
AI.result: The framework achieved 95.41% residue-level validation accuracy, 87.50% known-size exact-match accuracy, and 100% top-5 recovery on seven CAH2 known-mass benchmark cases.
AI.conclusion: The framework effectively reconstructs missing protein regions by integrating local sequence learning, homologous evidence, peptide mass constraints, and biochemical validation.

title: Representation learning of human cortical folding to reveal long lasting neurodevelopmental signatures
summary: The human brain folds in utero, primarily during late gestation. Shortly after birth, cortical folding patterns are established and remain stable thereafter, making them promising early neurodevelopmental markers. Yet it is unclear whether representations given by current neuroimaging foundation models capture cortical folding variability. Here, we introduce Champollion, a self-supervised learning framework that learns interpretable local representations of cortical folding from structural MRI. Optimized on representative folding-related tasks, Champollion accurately captures known folding patterns across cortical regions and external datasets. In a comprehensive benchmark, it consistently outperforms neuroimaging and general-purpose foundation models. Furthermore, Champollion reveals richer genetic associations than conventional morphometric descriptors and identifies localized folding signatures associated with incomplete hippocampal inversion, prematurity, and maternal smoking. These results establish cortical folding as a rich and largely untapped source of neurodevelopmental information and illustrate how pre-processing and architectural inductive biases can recover biologically meaningful signals overlooked by current generalist foundation models.

AI.tldr: Champollion is a self-supervised learning framework that learns interpretable local representations of cortical folding from structural MRI, outperforming existing foundation models on folding-related tasks and revealing new genetic and neurodevelopmental associations.
AI.motivation: Cortical folding patterns are established shortly after birth and remain stable, making them promising neurodevelopmental markers. However, it is unclear whether current neuroimaging foundation models capture cortical folding variability, as folding is a largely untapped source of information.
AI.method: Champollion uses a self-supervised learning framework to learn interpretable local representations of cortical folding from structural MRI, incorporating pre-processing and architectural inductive biases optimized for representative folding-related tasks.
AI.result: Champollion accurately captures known folding patterns across cortical regions and external datasets, consistently outperforms neuroimaging and general-purpose foundation models in a comprehensive benchmark, and reveals richer genetic associations than conventional morphometric descriptors. It also identifies localized folding signatures associated with incomplete hippocampal inversion, prematurity, and maternal smoking.
AI.conclusion: Cortical folding is a rich and largely untapped source of neurodevelopmental information. Pre-processing and architectural inductive biases can recover biologically meaningful signals that are overlooked by current generalist foundation models.

title: Precise Positional Readout of Molecular Barcode Structures using Solid-State Nanopores
summary: Fast and nonuniform translocation through solid-state nanopores limits both the detection of small molecular labels and their precise localization along molecular carriers. In this work we report the detection and localization performance of nucleotide-based molecular labels along double-stranded DNA scaffolds using solid-state nanopores in thin planar membranes. For small labels that are challenging to resolve individually, we introduce an anchoring strategy where readily detectable bulky labels serve as reference points to align multiple translocation events, enabling population-based detection and localization of smaller molecular features. The measured anchor positions constrain a probabilistic model of translocation velocity, identifying the most probable velocity profile for each event and enabling nonlinear trace "unwarping" for improved multi-event alignment. A complementary window-based evidence aggregation procedure accumulates weak but consistent label signatures across events, enabling detection of features that are individually masked by noise. These approaches enable robust recovery of single-dumbbell labels (DB1) on the order of 28 nucleotides and reduce mean localization errors to as low as 10 base pairs for DB3 labels and 40 base pairs for DB1 labels when averaging over multiple events. Stronger fractional DNA-associated current blockades, used as proxy for smaller pore geometries, are additionally associated with improved detection and lower localization error across membrane-based nanopore fabrication techniques. Overall, anchor-guided alignment provides a route to higher-density molecular information readout without compromising throughput via controlled translocation approaches.

AI.tldr: This paper presents anchor-guided alignment strategies to improve detection and localization of small nucleotide-based molecular labels along DNA scaffolds using solid-state nanopores in thin planar membranes, overcoming challenges of fast and nonuniform translocation.
AI.motivation: Fast and nonuniform translocation through solid-state nanopores limits detection of small molecular labels and their precise localization along molecular carriers, making it difficult to resolve small labels individually.
AI.method: Introduces an anchoring strategy using readily detectable bulky labels as reference points to align multiple translocation events. A probabilistic model of translocation velocity constrained by measured anchor positions enables nonlinear trace "unwarping" for improved multi-event alignment. A window-based evidence aggregation procedure accumulates weak label signatures across events to detect features masked by noise.
AI.result: Enables robust recovery of single-dumbbell labels (DB1) of ~28 nucleotides, reduces mean localization errors to as low as 10 base pairs for DB3 labels and 40 base pairs for DB1 labels when averaging over multiple events. Stronger fractional DNA-associated current blockades (proxy for smaller pore geometries) are associated with improved detection and lower localization error.
AI.conclusion: Anchor-guided alignment provides a route to higher-density molecular information readout without compromising throughput via controlled translocation approaches.

title: SureRoute: Toward a Hallucination-Free Self-Improving Platform for Retrosynthesis
summary: AI models, including large language models, are increasingly integrated into scientific discovery workflows, yet they remain prone to hallucination. In experimental sciences, such errors translate directly into failed wet-lab validations and wasted resources; in self-improving agentic systems, confident errors risk being reinforced rather than corrected. Retrosynthesis provides a representative example of this failure mode: existing models can generate chemically plausible routes, but cannot reliably determine which routes are experimentally feasible. We define \textbf{Chemical Hallucination} as a route that appears valid yet fails under competing reactive sites, unresolved selectivity, or missing mechanistic support, a failure largely invisible to the Recall@$K$ metric. We introduce \textbf{SureRoute}, a chemical verifier-anchored retrosynthesis platform that suppresses Chemical Hallucination. SureRoute combines a multi-model ensemble, data asset retrieval, and \textbf{ChemHarness}, an executable chemical intuition engine for route verification and reliability-first ranking. On a benchmark of 350 real-world industrial targets, SureRoute reaches 74.3\% recall@1, 2.2--3.5$\times$ that of seven single-step models and three frontier LLMs, while cutting top-1 Chemical Hallucination to 4.6\%, a 4--6$\times$ reduction relative to frontier LLMs. As a model-agnostic reranker, ChemHarness drives detectable hallucination toward near-zero across arbitrary backbone candidates. SureRoute shows that reliable scientific AI requires not only strong generation, but executable verification.

AI.tldr: SureRoute is a chemical verifier-anchored retrosynthesis platform that suppresses Chemical Hallucination—routes that appear valid but fail experimentally—by combining multi-model ensembles, data retrieval, and ChemHarness, an executable chemical intuition engine. On 350 industrial targets, it achieves 74.3% recall@1 and cuts hallucination to 4.6%.
AI.motivation: AI models in scientific discovery hallucinate; in experimental sciences this causes failed wet-lab validations and wasted resources, and in self-improving agentic systems confident errors risk reinforcement. Retrosynthesis models generate chemically plausible routes but cannot determine experimental feasibility, a failure invisible to Recall@K.
AI.method: SureRoute combines a multi-model ensemble, data asset retrieval, and ChemHarness—an executable chemical intuition engine for route verification and reliability-first ranking. ChemHarness serves as a model-agnostic reranker driving detectable hallucination toward near-zero across arbitrary backbone candidates.
AI.result: On 350 real-world industrial targets, SureRoute achieves 74.3% recall@1 (2.2–3.5× that of seven single-step models and three frontier LLMs) while cutting top-1 Chemical Hallucination to 4.6% (4–6× reduction relative to frontier LLMs).
AI.conclusion: Reliable scientific AI requires not only strong generation but executable verification; the verifier-anchored approach demonstrates that hallucination can be substantially suppressed through ensemble generation combined with executable chemical reasoning.

title: ZetaDial: dialing net charge of protein binders at inference time for therapeutic developability
summary: Net charge is a developability-relevant property of therapeutic binders, linked to viscosity, clearance, nonspecific interaction and aggregation, and antibody screens already use charge-related criteria. Yet inverse-folding pipelines expose no way to set it to a target value. ProteinMPNN and BindCraft offer amino-acid biases, weight choices and custom losses, but neither supplies a per-protein feedback loop that measures realised charge after sampling and corrects it to a setpoint. ZetaDial contributes a post-sampling, per-protein secant controller around fixed-backbone ProteinMPNN. On matched stochastic benchmarks the secant loop reduced mean absolute error relative to a fixed-slope loop on RCSB complexes (5.17 vs 6.46 charge units) and Cas13 monomers (5.57 vs 8.23). Relative to the optimised matched global bias, it cut RCSB error from 11.71 to 5.17 (cluster bootstrap p < 0.001) and was statistically indistinguishable on Cas13 (5.47 vs 5.57). Across 800 eight-protein subsets, sensitivity heterogeneity was associated with calibration gain (Pearson r = 0.79); this is descriptive resampling, not a prospective decision rule. Foldability deteriorated as bias magnitude increased. In the full 52-complex seed-0 analysis, reference-based DockQ declined clearly at +/-3 but not at +/-1.5; a selected five-seed replication on eight complexes showed paired declines at every nonzero setting, but does not estimate the effect for all 52. In exploratory BindCraft sweeps, PD-L1 designs moved toward near-neutral charge at similar maximum interface pTM but with overlapping success-rate intervals; IL-7R-alpha responses were non-monotonic and RBD produced no strong designs. A fixed-backbone C-alpha-neighbour analysis found smaller same-sign charge-patch proxies near neutral charge, but this proxy is not a measured electrostatic surface or experimental developability endpoint.

AI.tldr: ZetaDial is a post-sampling, per-protein secant controller for fixed-backbone ProteinMPNN that measures realized net charge after sampling and corrects it toward a setpoint, reducing mean absolute charge error versus fixed-slope and fixed global-bias baselines on RCSB and Cas13 benchmarks, though with observed trade-offs in foldability and limited generalizability of exploratory findings.
AI.motivation: Net charge is a developability-relevant property of therapeutic binders (linked to viscosity, clearance, nonspecific interaction, aggregation), and antibody screens already use charge-related criteria. However, existing inverse-folding pipelines such as ProteinMPNN and BindCraft provide amino-acid biases, weight choices, and custom losses, but no per-protein feedback loop that measures realized charge after sampling and corrects it to a setpoint.
AI.method: ZetaDial introduces a post-sampling, per-protein secant controller around fixed-backbone ProteinMPNN. It uses a feedback loop that measures the realized net charge after each sampling round and applies a secant-based correction to drive charge toward a target setpoint. Benchmarks were conducted against fixed-slope loops and optimized matched global biases on RCSB complexes and Cas13 monomers, with additional exploratory BindCraft sweeps on PD-L1, IL-7R-alpha, and RBD targets.
AI.result: The secant loop reduced mean absolute error relative to a fixed-slope loop on RCSB complexes (5.17 vs 6.46) and Cas13 monomers (5.57 vs 8.23). It outperformed the optimized matched global bias on RCSB (5.17 vs 11.71, p<0.001) and was statistically indistinguishable on Cas13 (5.47 vs 5.57). Calibration gain was associated with sensitivity heterogeneity (r=0.79). Foldability and DockQ deteriorated with larger bias magnitudes; DockQ declined at +/-3 but not +/-1.5 in the full 52-complex analysis. Exploratory sweeps showed PD-L1 designs moving toward near-neutral charge with comparable interface pTM, non-monotonic IL-7R-alpha responses, and no strong RBD designs.
AI.conclusion: ZetaDial demonstrates that per-protein feedback control of net charge is feasible and reduces charge error relative to static-bias baselines, but the approach entails trade-offs with foldability at larger bias magnitudes. Several findings are explicitly descriptive (e.g., sensitivity heterogeneity) or exploratory (e.g., BindCraft sweeps, five-seed replication), and the charge-patch analysis uses a proxy rather than measured electrostatic surface or experimental developability endpoints, limiting the strength of broader conclusions.

title: Slow fluctuations shape cell signaling near a bifurcation in embryonic stem cells
summary: Excitable and oscillatory responses are widespread in cell signaling, but how these arise in the same system is unclear. We propose a minimal model of a saddle node bifurcation on an invariant circle, where slow fluctuations modulate transitions between excitable and oscillatory states, and noise drives excitability. Fitting the model to cell signaling data from embryonic stem cells reveals that these cells operate close to the bifurcation. Proximity to the bifurcation allows the cell to tune different dynamic states, suggesting a general principle for versatile cell signaling.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a minimal model (saddle-node bifurcation on an invariant circle) where slow fluctuations and noise modulate transitions between excitable and oscillatory states in cell signaling. Fitting to embryonic stem cell data shows cells operate near the bifurcation, enabling versatile dynamic signaling.
AI.motivation: Excitable and oscillatory responses are both widespread in cell signaling, but how a single system can produce both types of dynamics is not well understood.
AI.method: A minimal model of a saddle-node bifurcation on an invariant circle (SNIC) is proposed, where slow fluctuations modulate the system between excitable and oscillatory regimes, with noise driving excitability. The model is fitted to cell signaling data from embryonic stem cells.
AI.result: Fitting the model to embryonic stem cell signaling data reveals that cells operate close to the bifurcation point, allowing them to access both excitable and oscillatory dynamic states.
AI.conclusion: Proximity to the bifurcation enables cells to flexibly tune between different dynamic states, suggesting a general principle for versatile and adaptable cell signaling.

title: Condition aware learning enables robust prediction of oligonucleotide melting behavior across diverse chemistries and assay conditions
summary: Oligonucleotide melting temperature is a fundamental determinant of nucleic acid hybridization and underpins the design of molecular diagnostics, polymerase chain reaction assays, and many other biotechnology applications. However, accurately predicting melting behavior remains difficult because it depends not only on sequence composition, but also on experimental conditions and chemical modifications commonly used in modern assay design. Existing thermodynamic models rely on fixed parameterizations that are often difficult to extend across diverse reaction environments and nucleotide chemistries. Here we show that a condition-aware nucleotide language model can accurately predict oligonucleotide melting behavior across diverse experimental conditions and both unmodified and chemically modified oligonucleotides. By combining contextual sequence representations with explicit information describing the reaction environment, the framework achieves sub-degree prediction accuracy and reduces prediction error for locked nucleic acid-modified oligonucleotides by up to 25% relative to nearest-neighbor thermodynamic approaches. The model also more accurately captures the thermal effects introduced by nucleotide modification and maintains strong performance on independent benchmark datasets spanning experimental conditions substantially different from those represented during training. Our results demonstrate that learned sequence representations can complement classical thermodynamic models by capturing context-dependent effects that are difficult to encode using fixed parameter tables alone. More broadly, this work provides a scalable framework for predicting oligonucleotide melting behavior across diverse chemistries and assay conditions, supporting more reliable molecular assay design.

AI.tldr: The authors present a condition-aware nucleotide language model that predicts oligonucleotide melting temperature with sub-degree accuracy across diverse experimental conditions and chemical modifications, achieving up to 25% error reduction for LNA-modified oligonucleotides compared to nearest-neighbor thermodynamic methods.
AI.motivation: Accurately predicting oligonucleotide melting temperature is critical for designing molecular diagnostics, PCR assays, and biotechnology applications, but existing thermodynamic models rely on fixed parameterizations that struggle to generalize across diverse reaction environments and nucleotide chemistries (e.g., chemical modifications like LNA).
AI.method: A condition-aware nucleotide language model combines contextual sequence representations (learned from nucleotide sequences) with explicit information about the reaction environment to predict melting behavior. This integrates learned sequence embeddings with condition descriptors, allowing the model to capture context-dependent effects that fixed parameter tables cannot encode.
AI.result: The model achieves sub-degree prediction accuracy, reduces prediction error for LNA-modified oligonucleotides by up to 25% relative to nearest-neighbor thermodynamic approaches, more accurately captures thermal effects of nucleotide modifications, and maintains strong performance on independent benchmark datasets with conditions substantially different from training.
AI.conclusion: Learned sequence representations can complement classical thermodynamic models by capturing context-dependent effects that are difficult to encode with fixed parameters, providing a scalable framework for predicting oligonucleotide melting behavior across diverse chemistries and assay conditions for more reliable molecular assay design.

title: PSLL: Persistent Sheaf Laplacian Learning for Protein-Ligand Binding Affinity Prediction
summary: Accurate prediction of protein-ligand binding affinity remains a central challenge in computational drug discovery due to the complex interplay among molecular geometry, physicochemical interactions, and atom-specific charge information. In this work, we introduce a Persistent Sheaf Laplacian learning (PSLL) framework for protein-ligand binding affinity prediction. The proposed approach constructs multiscale topological representations from three-dimensional protein-ligand complexes by incorporating atomic partial charges into sheaf restriction maps over Vietoris-Rips and alpha complex filtrations. To capture chemically diverse protein-ligand interactions, we introduce element-specific and category-specific atom-pair representations within the PSLL framework. Harmonic and non-harmonic spectra extracted from the resulting persistent sheaf Laplacians are used as molecular descriptors. To complement the PSLL-derived molecular representation, we incorporate transformer-based protein embeddings and SMILES-derived ligand descriptors for binding affinity prediction. The scoring power of the proposed multiscale PSLL model is validated against existing state-of-the-art methods on three widely used PDBbind benchmark datasets, including PDBbind-v2007, PDBbind-v2013, and PDBbind-v2016. The computational results indicate that the proposed PSLL model achieves strong predictive performance across benchmark datasets, highlighting its potential as an interpretable and mathematically grounded framework with promising generalizability for molecular machine learning and drug discovery.

AI.tldr: Introduces a Persistent Sheaf Laplacian learning (PSLL) framework for predicting protein-ligand binding affinity, which constructs multiscale topological representations by incorporating atomic partial charges into sheaf Laplacians over geometric filtrations, combined with transformer-based protein embeddings and SMILES-derived ligand descriptors, and validated on PDBbind benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Accurate protein-ligand binding affinity prediction is challenging due to the complex interplay of molecular geometry, physicochemical interactions, and atom-specific charge information, and existing methods struggle to capture these diverse factors effectively.
AI.method: The PSLL framework builds multiscale topological representations from 3D protein-ligand complexes using persistent sheaf Laplacians with atomic partial charges incorporated into sheaf restriction maps over Vietoris-Rips and alpha complex filtrations. It employs element-specific and category-specific atom-pair representations, extracts harmonic and non-harmonic spectral descriptors, and complements these with transformer-based protein embeddings and SMILES-derived ligand descriptors for binding affinity prediction.
AI.result: The PSLL model achieves strong predictive performance surpassing state-of-the-art methods across PDBbind-v2007, PDBbind-v2013, and PDBbind-v2016 benchmark datasets.
AI.conclusion: The PSLL framework demonstrates strong predictive accuracy and generalizability as an interpretable, mathematically grounded approach with promising potential for molecular machine learning and drug discovery applications.

title: Optimal long-run control of endemic infections: bang-bang threshold policies in a stochastic SIS model
summary: We study long-run optimal intervention strategies for endemic infections in a stochastic susceptible-infected-susceptible (SIS) model. The proportion of infected individuals evolves as a diffusion process with random fluctuations, while a control variable $ζ_t\in[0,\tildeζ_{max}]$ represents the intensity of public health interventions that reduce transmission for some intervention threshold $\tildeζ_{max}\in (0,1]$. The objective is to minimize the long-run average societal cost, balancing the burden of infection against the costs of interventions. Under a concave intervention cost structure the problem can be formulated as an ergodic stochastic control problem, whose structure implies (under certain additional conditions) that optimal interventions are of bang-bang type, switching between no intervention and the maximal admissible intervention at a single switching threshold in the infection level. We construct candidate value functions, rigorously verify optimality in this single-threshold case, and relate the results to extinction and persistence properties of the underlying SIS dynamics in the absence of control. In our framework, the analysis provides a rigorous justification for the threshold-based intervention rules commonly used in epidemic management.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes long-run optimal intervention strategies for endemic infections in a stochastic SIS model where the infection proportion follows a diffusion process. Under concave intervention costs, the problem becomes an ergodic stochastic control problem yielding optimal bang-bang policies (switching between no intervention and maximal intervention at a single infection threshold). The authors construct candidate value functions, rigorously verify optimality, and relate results to extinction/persistence of unconstrained SIS dynamics, justifying threshold-based intervention rules used in practice.
AI.motivation: Public health authorities commonly use threshold-based intervention rules (act when infection levels cross critical levels), yet rigorous justification of such policies in epidemic management is lacking. This work aims to provide a mathematical foundation for these practical intervention strategies by studying them in a stochastic SIS epidemic framework.
AI.method: The authors model the infected proportion as a diffusion process with a control variable representing intervention intensity within [0, ζ_max]. They formulate a long-run average cost minimization problem with concave intervention costs as an ergodic stochastic control problem. Under structural conditions, they derive that optimal policies are bang-bang (switching between no intervention and maximal intervention at a single threshold). They construct candidate value functions and rigorously verify their optimality.
AI.result: Optimal interventions are of bang-bang type with a single switching threshold in the infection level. Candidate value functions are constructed and verified for optimality in the single-threshold case. Results are connected to extinction and persistence properties of the uncontrolled SIS dynamics, providing rigorous justification for threshold-based intervention rules.
AI.conclusion: The framework rigorously justifies threshold-based intervention policies commonly used in epidemic management, showing that under concave costs and certain structural conditions, the optimal long-run strategy is to apply maximal intervention intensity when infection crosses a single critical threshold and no intervention otherwise.

title: Orchestra: Corroboration-Based Regulatory Candidate Discovery via Composed Bioinformatics MCP Agents
summary:
Orchestra composes two independently built bioinformatics MCP servers -- RegNetAgents, which infers gene regulatory
  network topology from ARACNe networks, and CASCADE, which supplies four independent evidence sources (LINCS knockdown,
  DepMap essentiality, super-enhancer status, DoRothEA transcription-factor confidence) -- into one multi-agent
  workflow exposed via the Model Context Protocol. Its central architectural claim is that requiring RegNetAgents'
  topology evidence and CASCADE's experimental evidence to agree on a candidate regulator yields a more trustworthy
  candidate than either alone -- not previously tested directly, since RegNetAgents' own validation asked only whether
  its candidate lists beat chance.
  We test this on the TCGA tumor-acquired regulator tier (regulators in a gene's tumor ARACNe network but absent from
  the GREmLN population-averaged baseline), selecting candidates by ARACNe mutual-information (MI) edge weight. On
  RegNetAgents' published BRCA/COAD focal-gene panel plus matched negative controls, agreement among at least 2 of the 4
  CASCADE sources predicts OncoKB cancer-gene status among focal genes (odds ratio 2.89, Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted
  p=0.0166) but not among negative controls (p=0.0721); a single source is not diagnostic for either group. The pattern
  replicates and strengthens in a third cancer type, STAD, on a separately constructed panel (odds ratio 5.82), and
  against an independently curated ground truth (the Sanger COSMIC Cancer Gene Census). MI edge weight is the strongest
  single predictor overall (p=0.0003); a logistic-regression likelihood-ratio test confirms corroboration adds value
  beyond it in both panels (p=0.0234; p=0.0001). Every experiment invokes Orchestra's real agentic entry point.

AI.tldr: Orchestra integrates two independently built bioinformatics MCP servers (RegNetAgents for gene regulatory network topology inference and CASCADE for four experimental evidence sources) into a multi-agent workflow. The paper tests whether requiring agreement between topology evidence and experimental evidence produces more trustworthy candidate regulators than either alone, finding that agreement among at least 2 of 4 CASCADE sources predicts cancer-gene status across multiple cancer types and validation panels.
AI.motivation: RegNetAgents' own validation only asked whether its candidate lists beat chance, but never tested whether combining its topology evidence with independent experimental evidence yields more trustworthy candidates. The paper addresses this gap by testing whether corroboration between topology inference and experimental evidence improves candidate reliability.
AI.method: Orchestra composes RegNetAgents (ARACNe-based gene regulatory network topology inference) and CASCADE (four evidence sources: LINCS knockdown, DepMap essentiality, super-enhancer status, DoRothEA TF confidence) into a multi-agent workflow via the Model Context Protocol. Candidates from the TCGA tumor-acquired regulator tier are selected by ARACNe mutual-information edge weight, tested on BRCA/COAD focal-gene panels with matched negative controls and a separately constructed STAD panel.
AI.result: Agreement among at least 2 of 4 CASCADE sources predicts OncoKB cancer-gene status among focal genes (odds ratio 2.89, adjusted p=0.0166) but not negative controls (p=0.0721). Results replicate in STAD (odds ratio 5.82) and against COSMIC Cancer Gene Census. MI edge weight is the strongest single predictor (p=0.0003); logistic-regression likelihood-ratio tests confirm corroboration adds value beyond it (p=0.0234; p=0.0001).
AI.conclusion: Cross-source corroboration between topology and experimental evidence meaningfully improves candidate regulator trustworthiness, and corroboration adds predictive value beyond single features like mutual-information edge weight alone.

title: A Network-Based Biomarker of Morphological Disruption Associated with Breast Cancer Malignancy
summary: Breast cancer diagnosis commonly considers individual nuclear morphological characteristics, whereas their joint organization is less frequently evaluated. We developed the Morphological Network Disruption Index (MNDI), a patient-level measure of morphological abnormality relative to a benign reference state. Using the Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer dataset, ten nuclear characteristics were represented as network nodes, with MNDI summarizing disruption across 45 pairwise feature configurations. Performance was evaluated using repeated stratified five-fold cross-validation. Malignant lesions exhibited substantially higher MNDI than benign lesions (mean: 3.454 vs. 1.165; p = 2.94e-69). MNDI achieved an AUC of 0.941 (95% CI: 0.918-0.961), with 85.9% sensitivity and 91.6% specificity. A classifier using network-derived descriptors achieved an AUC of AUC of 0.928 +/- 0.024. Independent evaluation in the BreaKHis histopathology cohort showed limited discrimination (AUC = 0.538, 95% CI: 0.401-0.668), indicating dependence on the underlying morphological representation. MNDI provides an interpretable framework for quantifying patient-specific morphological disruption, while individual implementations require validation within compatible feature spaces.

AI.tldr: The authors propose the Morphological Network Disruption Index (MNDI), a patient-level metric quantifying breast cancer morphological abnormality via network analysis of ten nuclear features across 45 pairwise configurations. MNDI significantly distinguishes malignant from benign lesions (AUC=0.941) on the Wisconsin dataset but generalizes poorly to BreaKHis (AUC=0.538), highlighting feature-space dependence.
AI.motivation: Breast cancer diagnosis typically evaluates individual nuclear morphological characteristics in isolation, overlooking their joint or networked organization. The authors aim to capture the collective disruption of morphological relationships, which may provide additional diagnostic information beyond single-feature assessments.
AI.method: Ten nuclear characteristics from the Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer dataset are modeled as network nodes. MNDI summarizes morphological disruption across all 45 pairwise feature configurations relative to a benign reference state. Performance is evaluated via repeated stratified five-fold cross-validation, with independent validation on the BreaKHis histopathology cohort.
AI.result: Malignant lesions showed substantially higher MNDI than benign (mean 3.454 vs 1.165; p=2.94e-69). MNDI achieved AUC=0.941 (95% CI: 0.918-0.961) with 85.9% sensitivity and 91.6% specificity. A network-derived classifier reached AUC=0.928±0.024. Independent BreaKHis evaluation showed poor discrimination (AUC=0.538), indicating dependence on underlying morphological representation.
AI.conclusion: MNDI offers an interpretable patient-level framework for quantifying morphological network disruption in breast cancer. However, its performance is highly dependent on the feature space used, necessitating validation within compatible morphological representations before clinical deployment across different imaging modalities or cohorts.

title: Spread of Chronic Wasting Disease under Stochastic Environmental Conditions and its Control using Deep Reinforcement Learning
summary: Chronic wasting disease (CWD) is a fatal prion disease affecting deer, elk, moose, reindeer, muntjac, and other cervids. Because free-ranging cervid populations face environmental variability and randomness, deterministic models may miss important dynamics like stochastic fade-out. We develop a stochastic Susceptible-Infectious-Environmental model using differential equations with reflection to ensure the susceptible class remains non-negative. We examine how environmental variability influences cervid populations as CWD pressure and control measures increase. For the deterministic model, we derive the basic reproduction number as the sum of direct and environmental contributions, showing the endemic phase arises at R0=1. For the stochastic system, we establish local well-posedness, positivity, and the disease-free law. The top Lyapunov exponent for invasion remains unaffected by reflection. We evaluate CWD mitigation using a deep reinforcement learning agent trained with Proximal Policy Optimization in a hybrid action space, comparing hunting, decontamination, and combined strategies. In the deterministic case, hunting alone can control the disease but reduces the population by about 58%, while decontamination requires sustained effort. The combined policy more than doubles the cervid population and nearly eliminates infection and contamination. In the stochastic case, the policy contains the disease in about 80% of runs, with 10% experiencing large outbreaks; effectiveness decreases as noise increases. Across all scenarios, the agent consistently emphasizes environmental decontamination, the key control method.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a stochastic Susceptible-Infectious-Environmental model with reflection for chronic wasting disease in cervids, derives the basic reproduction number for the deterministic case, establishes stochastic system properties (well-posedness, positivity, disease-free law), and evaluates CWD mitigation via deep reinforcement learning (PPO) comparing hunting, decontamination, and combined strategies in both deterministic and stochastic settings.
AI.motivation: Free-ranging cervid populations face environmental variability and randomness, so deterministic models may miss important dynamics such as stochastic fade-out. The authors aim to capture these dynamics and assess how environmental variability influences population outcomes as CWD pressure and control efforts increase.
AI.method: Develops a stochastic Susceptible-Infectious-Environmental model using differential equations with reflection to keep the susceptible class non-negative. Derives the basic reproduction number for the deterministic model as a sum of direct and environmental contributions. Establishes local well-posedness, positivity, and disease-free law for the stochastic system, and examines the top Lyapunov exponent for invasion. Evaluates CWD mitigation using a deep reinforcement learning agent trained with Proximal Policy Optimization in a hybrid action space, comparing hunting, decontamination, and combined strategies.
AI.result: Deterministic model shows endemic phase arises at R0=1. Hunting alone can control disease but reduces population by ~58%; decontamination requires sustained effort. The combined policy more than doubles the cervid population and nearly eliminates infection and contamination. In the stochastic case, the policy contains the disease in ~80% of runs, with 10% experiencing large outbreaks; effectiveness decreases as noise increases. Across all scenarios the agent consistently emphasizes environmental decontamination as the key control method.
AI.conclusion: The stochastic model captures important disease dynamics missed by deterministic approaches, and combined hunting and decontamination strategies vastly outperform either alone. Environmental decontamination emerges as the most critical control measure, though stochastic noise can undermine effectiveness in some runs.

title: Modeling Medea gene-drive population replacement: thresholds and release strategies
summary: Mosquito-borne diseases such as dengue, Zika, and yellow fever impose a substantial global health burden, motivating genetic control strategies that replace wild mosquito populations with disease-refractory ones. Maternal-effect dominant embryonic arrest (Medea) is a gene drive in which the offspring of a Medea-carrying mother die unless they inherit the Medea allele, producing biased inheritance capable of driving a linked refractory trait to high prevalence. We develop and analyze a continuous-time compartmental model of Medea dynamics in Aedes aegypti that tracks mosquito abundance by life stage and genotype, and that generalizes the drive mechanism to allow both imperfect Medea-killing and imperfect rescue. We characterize the biologically relevant equilibria and derive their local stability conditions, together with genotype-specific reproduction numbers and the basic reproduction number (R0) governing invasion from low frequency. Bifurcation analysis reveals bistability, and hence a release threshold that must be exceeded for Medea to take over, even though R0<1 at baseline. Imperfect killing and imperfect rescue reshape this bifurcation structure in distinct ways: killing leakage governs the invasion threshold, while rescue efficiency governs the composition of the resulting population. Sensitivity analysis identifies the fitness coefficient and killing leakage as the dominant drivers of both threshold and coverage outcomes, with mosquito demographic parameters affecting absolute abundances but not genotype proportions. Simulations of batched release programs inform efficient field deployment and show that reversing an established drive is substantially more costly than achieving forward invasion, though co-releasing both sexes accelerates reversal considerably more than it accelerates invasion.

AI.tldr: A continuous-time compartmental model of Medea gene drive dynamics in Aedes aegypti is developed, tracking mosquitoes by life stage and genotype, revealing bistability with a release threshold, distinct effects of imperfect killing vs. rescue, and practical insights for field deployment and drive reversal.
AI.motivation: Mosquito-borne diseases (dengue, Zika, yellow fever) create a substantial global health burden, motivating genetic control strategies to replace wild mosquito populations with disease-refractory ones. Understanding Medea gene drive dynamics mathematically is essential for designing effective and safe interventions.
AI.method: A continuous-time compartmental model tracks mosquito abundance by life stage and genotype, generalizing Medea to allow imperfect killing and imperfect rescue. Analysis includes equilibrium characterization, local stability conditions, genotype-specific reproduction numbers, R0, bifurcation analysis, and sensitivity analysis. Batched release simulations inform deployment strategies.
AI.result: Bistability creates a release threshold for Medea takeover even when R0<1 at baseline. Imperfect killing (leakage) governs the invasion threshold, while imperfect rescue governs population composition. Sensitivity analysis identifies fitness coefficient and killing leakage as dominant drivers. Simulations show co-releasing both sexes accelerates reversal much more than invasion, and reversing an established drive is far more costly than achieving forward invasion.
AI.conclusion: Mathematical modeling reveals critical operational constraints for Medea-based mosquito control: killing leakage determines whether Medea can invade, rescue efficiency determines final outcomes, and practical deployment strategies (including sex ratios in releases) must be optimized—with reversal being inherently more difficult than forward invasion.

title: Kuramoto Phase Synchronization in Regional Epidemic Dynamics: Two Test Cases from European COVID-19 and Influenza Surveillance
summary: We test whether the Kuramoto model quantitatively describes spatial synchronization in regional epidemic waves, using daily COVID-19 incidence for 400 German \emph{Kreise} (2021--2023) and weekly ILI rates for 12 European countries (ECDC, 2021--2026). Bandpass filtering and Hilbert-transform phase extraction yield high global order parameters ($\langle r\rangle\approx0.87$ for Germany; $\langle r\rangle\approx0.97$ for Europe), yet both are dominated by a common-mode driver rather than pairwise local coupling. Removing the common mode reveals genuine short-range synchronization: an exponentially decaying residual local order with correlation length $ξ=152\pm6$~km in Germany, and a significant neighbor-vs.-non-neighbor contrast (Mann--Whitney $p=0.005$) in the European panel. We interpret this convergent pattern across two diseases and two spatial scales as a universal two-scale structure: a long-range common-mode field superimposed on shorter-range diffusive coupling. Cross-validation against a companion gauge-mediated Doi--Peliti framework shows that district-level effective screening mass $m_R$ is uncorrelated with local~$r$ (null result), the national $(m_R,r)$ phase portrait independently reproduces a previously reported hysteresis loop, and pairwise phase lags quantitatively match fractional-calculus predictions. A frequency--degree correlation provides the structural signature of explosive synchronization; excess synchronization between districts sharing the same \emph{Bundesland} implicates shared school-holiday calendars and state-level policy as local coupling drivers.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether the Kuramoto model quantitatively describes spatial synchronization in regional epidemic waves using COVID-19 data from 400 German Kreise (2021-2023) and ILI data from 12 European countries (2021-2026). Results show high global order parameters dominated by a common-mode driver, with genuine short-range synchronization revealed after removing the common mode—an exponentially decaying local order with correlation length ξ=152±6 km in Germany and significant neighbor-vs-non-neighbor contrast in Europe. This converges to a universal two-scale structure: long-range common-mode field over short-range diffusive coupling. Cross-validation against a Doi-Peliti framework shows null results for local screening mass correlation, reproduces a hysteresis loop in the national phase portrait, and matches fractional-calculus predictions. Frequency-degree correlation indicates explosive synchronization, and excess synchronization within same Bundesland implicates school holidays and state policy as local drivers.
AI.motivation: To test whether the Kuramoto model provides a quantitative description of spatial synchronization in regional epidemic waves, addressing whether observed synchronization arises from local pairwise coupling or from a common external driver, and to establish a universal mechanistic framework applicable across diseases and spatial scales.
AI.method: Use daily COVID-19 incidence for 400 German Kreise (2021-2023) and weekly ILI rates for 12 European countries (ECDC, 2021-2026). Apply bandpass filtering and Hilbert-transform phase extraction. Compute global order parameters, remove common mode to isolate residual local synchronization, measure correlation lengths, and perform neighbor-vs-non-neighbor Mann-Whitney tests. Cross-validate against a gauge-mediated Doi-Peliti framework examining effective screening mass m_R correlations, phase portraits, and phase lags against fractional-calculus predictions. Analyze frequency-degree correlations and Bundesland-level synchronization.
AI.result: High global order parameters (r≈0.87 Germany, r≈0.97 Europe) dominated by common-mode drivers. After common-mode removal: exponential decay of residual local order with ξ=152±6 km in Germany; significant neighbor-vs-non-neighbor contrast (p=0.005) in Europe. Effective screening mass m_R uncorrelated with local r (null result); national (m_R,r) phase portrait reproduces previously reported hysteresis loop; pairwise phase lags match fractional-calculus predictions. Frequency-degree correlation provides structural signature of explosive synchronization; excess synchronization within same Bundesland implicates school-holiday calendars and state-level policy as local coupling drivers.
AI.conclusion: Epidemic spatial synchronization exhibits a universal two-scale structure: a long-range common-mode field superimposed on shorter-range diffusive coupling. The Kuramoto model quantitatively describes the local synchronization component after accounting for the common-mode driver, with convergent evidence across two diseases and two spatial scales. Local coupling is driven by shared school-holiday calendars and state-level policies rather than district-level screening effectiveness.

title: Synergistic Effects of Behavioral Feedback and Seasonality Generate Chaos in Cooperative Multi-Pathogen Systems
summary: Infectious diseases may interact by competing for the same hosts or by facilitating subsequent infections. Understanding the dynamics of such multi-pathogen systems, particularly those subject to endemic seasonality and mitigation, is essential for designing robust public health interventions. We propose a three-stage modeling framework to disentangle the interplay between seasonality and behavioral feedback as a way of mitigation. First, we analyze a coupled susceptible-infectious-recovered-susceptible (SIRS) system without external forcing and show that the abrupt transition between the disease-free and endemic equilibria arises from a backward bifurcation-induced first-order phase transition. Second, we independently examine seasonality and behavioral feedback, characterizing where and when oscillatory behavior is induced near critical tipping points. Third, we demonstrate that their combination generates complex multi-annual wave patterns, with high-incidence cycles driven by seasonality and low-incidence intervals driven by behavioral feedback. By mapping stability as a function of seasonal forcing, mitigation strength, and cooperativity, we identify distinct period-doubling cascades with chaotic signatures arising from different mechanisms: the interplay between seasonality and behavior, and inter-pathogen cooperativity with the backward bifurcation it induces. We then analyze how these mechanisms interact across parameter ranges. Altogether, we show that cooperation fundamentally expands the spectrum of possible epidemic patterns, highlighting the importance of considering multi-pathogen interactions in epidemic modeling and control strategies.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a three-stage modeling framework for multi-pathogen systems with seasonality and behavioral feedback, revealing that inter-pathogen cooperation fundamentally expands the spectrum of epidemic patterns, including phase transitions, oscillatory behavior, multi-annual waves, and period-doubling cascades with chaotic signatures.
AI.motivation: Infectious diseases can interact by competing for hosts or facilitating infections, but understanding multi-pathogen dynamics under endemic seasonality and mitigation is critical for robust public health interventions, and existing approaches do not adequately disentangle the interplay between seasonality and behavioral feedback.
AI.method: A three-stage modeling framework is used: (1) analyzing a coupled SIRS system without external forcing to show backward bifurcation-induced first-order phase transitions; (2) independently examining seasonality and behavioral feedback to characterize oscillatory behavior near critical tipping points; (3) demonstrating how their combination generates complex multi-annual wave patterns and mapping stability as a function of seasonal forcing, mitigation strength, and cooperativity to identify period-doubling cascades with chaotic signatures from distinct mechanisms.
AI.result: Cooperation expands the spectrum of possible epidemic patterns. The framework identifies high-incidence cycles driven by seasonality, low-incidence intervals driven by behavioral feedback, and distinct period-doubling cascades with chaotic signatures arising from different mechanisms: seasonality-behavior interplay versus inter-pathogen cooperativity with induced backward bifurcation.
AI.conclusion: Considering multi-pathogen interactions is important in epidemic modeling and control strategies, as cooperation fundamentally broadens the range of possible epidemic dynamical behaviors.

title: Determinants of hyperparameter robustness in connectome reservoir computing
comment: 20 pages, 12 figures, including supplementary material. Submitted to Neural Networks
summary:
Reservoir computing provides a controlled setting for studying how recurrent network architectureshapes computation: input signals are projected into a high-dimensional state space by a fixed nonlinear dynamical system, and only the readout is trained. However, reservoir performance can be dependent on hyperparameters; this paper asks which recurrent network features support robustness to those parameter changes. We characterize computational performance using memory capacity (MC), truncated single-delay information-processing capacity (IPC), and kernel rank (KR). Generalization across input histories is measured using generalization rank (GR), while hyperparameter robustness is quantified using the coefficient of variation (CV) of each metric across sweeps of target spectral radius, input scaling, leak rate, and neuron bias.
  To examine the architectural determinants of robustness, we construct perturbations that alter connectivity topology, excitatory/inhibitory sign structure, weight magnitudes, and weight placement while preserving complementary properties. Across these experiments, the C. elegans connectome consistently occupies a relatively low-variance regime.
  The central result is a performance-robustness tradeoff: architecture variants with higher task-agnostic performance also tend to exhibit greater hyperparameter sensitivity and poorer common-tail generalization. Across the E/I edge balance sweeps and shuffle controls, this tradeoff is closely associated with the raw spectral radius before normalization. Because every perturbed matrix is rescaled to the same target radius, matrices with lower raw spectral radius receive greater global amplification of their recurrent weights. The observed differences among architectures therefore characterize the joint effects of structural variation and architecture-specific global rescaling under spectral-radius normalization.

AI.tldr: This paper studies reservoir computing architectures to determine which recurrent network features promote robustness to hyperparameter changes. Using metrics like memory capacity, information-processing capacity, kernel rank, and generalization rank, the authors find that the C. elegans connectome occupies a low-variance regime. Their central finding is a performance-robustness tradeoff: architectures with higher task-agnostic performance show greater hyperparameter sensitivity and poorer generalization, largely driven by raw spectral radius before normalization and the global amplification applied during rescaling.
AI.motivation: Reservoir computing performance is often highly dependent on hyperparameter choices, yet it is unclear which architectural features of recurrent networks confer robustness to those parameter changes. The paper aims to identify structural determinants of robustness in reservoir computing systems.
AI.method: The authors characterize reservoirs using multiple metrics (MC, IPC, KR for performance; GR for generalization; CV for hyperparameter robustness). They construct perturbations that independently alter topology, E/I sign structure, weight magnitudes, and weight placement while preserving other properties. They sweep hyperparameters (spectral radius, input scaling, leak rate, neuron bias) and compare architecture variants, including the C. elegans connectome.
AI.result: The C. elegans connectome consistently displays relatively low variance across perturbations. A performance-robustness tradeoff emerges: higher task-agnostic performance correlates with greater hyperparameter sensitivity and poorer generalization. This tradeoff relates closely to raw spectral radius before normalization, since rescaling to a common target radius amplifies matrices with lower raw spectral radius more globally.
AI.conclusion: Architecture-specific differences in reservoir performance and robustness are jointly explained by structural variation and the global rescaling applied under spectral-radius normalization. The findings caution that performance gains may come at the cost of hyperparameter fragility and degraded generalization.

title: Human mutation field reveals an equilibrium-like structure with irreversible circulation
summary: The evolution of DNA sequences can be viewed as stochastic dynamics on a high-dimensional discrete space, but it is unclear when empirical transition biases reduce to an effective energy landscape versus retain irreducible non-equilibrium circulation. Human context-dependent mutation probabilities offer a direct test: every single-nucleotide substitution in a local context has a reverse substitution, so the logarithm of the forward-to-reverse probability ratio defines an antisymmetric field-the human mutation field. We show this field has a dominant gradient component and a smaller but reproducible curl component. Using seven-base human germline substitution probabilities, we infer an effective mutational landscape with a Siamese neural network constrained to predict only energy differences. This model predicts forward-to-reverse log-ratios for held-out mutations with a correlation of about 0.93, close to both an unconstrained predictive reference (0.948) and the empirical reversible ceiling from Hodge projection (about 0.96). Although trained only on mutation probabilities, the inferred landscape largely recovers short-word genomic composition and Chargaff reverse-complement symmetry for sequences up to length four. Deviations from equilibrium structure reveal a small but detectable nonequilibrium component: a residual irreversible circulation violating the Kolmogorov cycle condition for detailed balance, reproducible across African, Asian, and European populations, and strongest in CpG-linked cycles and CpG-transition edges, consistent with methylcytosine deamination. These results give a thermodynamic decomposition of the human mutation field: most mutation bias is organized by a local equilibrium-like energy landscape aligned with genome composition, while the residual circulation points to specific directional mutational mechanisms.

AI.tldr: This paper decomposes the human mutation field into an equilibrium-like energy landscape and a residual non-equilibrium circulation. Using seven-base substitution probabilities and a Siamese neural network constrained to predict energy differences, the authors recover an effective mutational landscape that accurately predicts forward-to-reverse log-ratios and largely reconstructs genomic composition, while a small but reproducible irreversible circulation (strongest in CpG-linked cycles) points to specific directional mechanisms like methylcytosine deamination.
AI.motivation: To determine whether empirical mutation transition biases in human DNA reduce to an effective energy landscape (equilibrium) or retain irreducible non-equilibrium circulation. This provides a thermodynamic understanding of how sequence evolution is organized.
AI.method: Defines the human mutation field as the log ratio of forward-to-reverse substitution probabilities. Uses Hodge decomposition to separate gradient (equilibrium) and curl (non-equilibrium) components. Trains a Siamese neural network constrained to predict only energy differences to infer an effective mutational landscape from seven-base germline substitution probabilities. Validates against held-out mutations and compares with predictive and reversible ceilings. Assesses recovery of short-word genomic composition and Chargaff symmetry. Examines residual circulation via Kolmogorov cycle conditions across populations.
AI.result: The mutation field has a dominant gradient component and a smaller reproducible curl. The neural network model predicts held-out forward-to-reverse log-ratios with correlation ~0.93 (near the unconstrained reference 0.948 and reversible ceiling ~0.96). The inferred landscape largely recovers short-word genomic composition and Chargaff reverse-complement symmetry for sequences up to length four. A small but detectable nonequilibrium circulation violates detailed balance, is reproducible across populations, and is strongest in CpG-linked cycles and CpG-transition edges, consistent with methylcytosine deamination.
AI.conclusion: The human mutation field decomposes thermodynamically: most mutation bias is organized by a local equilibrium-like energy landscape aligned with genome composition, while a residual circulation reveals specific directional mutational mechanisms such as methylcytosine deamination.

title: Homeostasis Revisited and Reformulated Through Hidden Markov Model Control
summary: A common formalization of homeostasis is the free energy principle, a framework that defines a set of desired observation values, or critical states, that the agent should reach or remain close to. Under the free energy principle, an agent should act to maximize the probability of receiving the desired observations. Here we revisit the common approach of solving the problem of maximizing the log probability of the desired observations by maximizing a variational lower bound, the so-called negative free energy. We show that, instead, an approach directly maximizing that probability under the agent's policy is better suited to, and provides a better solution for, the original homeostatic control problem. This is done using hidden Markov model (HMM) control by allowing the policy to act over hidden states or noisy versions thereof while trying to maximize the probability of repeatedly having the desired observations. HMM control largely improves performance over the variational, or free energy, approach. We also show that the optimal policy is strictly deterministic, while the variational approach leads to a stochastic policy approximation. We finally provide a homeostatic reinterpretation of the maximum occupancy principle -a principle proposing that agents ought to maximize the occupancy of action-state path space -by defining homeostatic states as any states that do not immediately entail the termination or death of the agent.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that directly maximizing the log probability of desired observations (homeostatic states) under an agent's policy, using hidden Markov model (HMM) control, outperforms the common free energy principle approach that maximizes a variational lower bound (negative free energy). The authors show HMM control achieves better performance, yields a strictly deterministic optimal policy (vs. stochastic approximation in the variational approach), and provides a homeostatic reinterpretation of the maximum occupancy principle.
AI.motivation: The free energy principle is commonly used to formalize homeostasis, framing agents as acting to maximize the probability of desired critical observations. However, the standard approach maximizes a variational lower bound (negative free energy) rather than the true log probability of desired observations, which may not be well suited to the original homeostatic control problem. The authors seek a more direct and principled solution to this problem.
AI.method: The authors propose HMM control, a framework where the policy acts over hidden states (or noisy versions thereof) while directly maximizing the probability of repeatedly observing desired (homeostatic) states. This is contrasted against the variational/free energy approach that maximizes a lower bound on the log probability of desired observations, using a hidden Markov model formalization.
AI.result: HMM control largely improves performance over the variational (free energy) approach. The optimal policy under direct maximization is shown to be strictly deterministic, whereas the variational approach yields only a stochastic policy approximation. The authors also provide a homeostatic reinterpretation of the maximum occupancy principle by defining homeostatic states as any states that do not immediately lead to the agent's termination or death.
AI.conclusion: Directly maximizing the probability of desired observations, as done in HMM control, is better suited to and provides a better solution for the homeostatic control problem than maximizing a variational bound. This challenges the adequacy of the free energy principle's common variational formulation and connects to a broader maximal occupancy view of homeostasis.

title: Numerical approximations of population size distributions for multi-type branching processes
summary: Continuous-time multi-type branching processes are fundamental models for expanding and migrating populations with cancer evolution being a prototypical example. Inferring model parameters, like mutation and growth rates, from time-series count data requires efficient computation of population size distributions. Existing methods are mainly based on large-time or large-number asymptotics, which rely on either restricted initial conditions or simplified interactions between cell types. Here, we introduce two numerical approximations of population size distributions for multi-type branching processes on directed graphs with arbitrary initialization. The first approach combines a saddle-point approximation with numerical integration of the probability generating function. We characterize admissibility and establish conditions for saddle-point existence and uniqueness. For directed acyclic graphs, the second approach provides a large-time small-mutation-rate alternative based on closed-form approximate Laplace transforms and efficient numerical inversion. We benchmark the accuracy and speed of both solutions in simulations, showing substantial improvement over the state-of-the-art large-number approximation and orders of magnitude speedup over Gillespie's stochastic simulation algorithm at matching accuracy. We apply our methods to analyze the relapse dynamics of an acute myeloid leukemia patient, where rapid parameter scans over a six-type patient-specific mutation tree quantify how unobserved remission burden and treatment-altered fitness can explain relapse. Our methods provide computational building blocks for future likelihood-based inference in cancer evolution and other expanding populations.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces two numerical approximations for computing population size distributions in continuous-time multi-type branching processes on directed graphs with arbitrary initialization: one combining saddle-point approximation with numerical integration of probability generating functions, and another using closed-form approximate Laplace transforms with efficient numerical inversion for directed acyclic graphs under large-time small-mutation-rate conditions. The methods show substantial accuracy improvements over existing large-number approximations and orders of magnitude speedup over Gillespie's stochastic simulation. They are applied to analyze acute myeloid leukemia relapse dynamics.
AI.motivation: Inferring model parameters like mutation and growth rates from time-series count data in cancer evolution requires efficient computation of population size distributions for multi-type branching processes. Existing methods rely on large-time or large-number asymptotics that have restricted initial conditions or simplified cell-type interactions, limiting their applicability.
AI.method: Two numerical approximation approaches are proposed: (1) A saddle-point approximation combined with numerical integration of the probability generating function, with characterized admissibility and conditions for saddle-point existence and uniqueness. (2) For directed acyclic graphs, a large-time small-mutation-rate alternative based on closed-form approximate Laplace transforms and efficient numerical inversion.
AI.result: Both solutions were benchmarked in simulations showing substantial improvement over the state-of-the-art large-number approximation and orders of magnitude speedup over Gillespie's stochastic simulation algorithm at comparable accuracy. Application to an acute myeloid leukemia patient's relapse dynamics demonstrated rapid parameter scans over a six-type patient-specific mutation tree, quantifying how unobserved remission burden and treatment-altered fitness explain relapse.
AI.conclusion: The proposed methods provide fast and accurate computational building blocks for likelihood-based inference in cancer evolution and other expanding populations, enabling analysis that was previously computationally prohibitive.

title: Fisher Information Metric as a model-free measure of proximity to criticality in neural systems
summary: Critical phenomena are widespread across many disciplines and have recently become a topic of deep interest in the study of biological and artificial neural networks. A distinct signature of criticality is the emergence of avalanches with power-law-distributed sizes and durations. However, empirically estimating the critical exponents remains challenging, and their interpretation is often model-dependent. In this work, we demonstrate how the Fisher Information Metric (FIM), a measure of generalized susceptibility, provides a comprehensive, model-agnostic characterization of the critical region in neural systems. We validate this approach across models of increasing biological complexity, from prototypical branching processes to spiking and whole-brain models, showing that FIM of each model's control parameter reliably tracks the system's degree of criticality. To emulate the study of real-world systems, where the control parameter is unknown, we additionally calculate FIM of the observed branching ratio of neural activity. The resulting FIM peaks where activity growth and decay balance, with the peak sharpening as the system approaches criticality. Hence, FIM peak width and height yield continuous, model-free readouts of proximity to criticality without requiring knowledge of the true control parameter, offering a robust tool for probing criticality in neural systems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using the Fisher Information Metric (FIM) as a model-agnostic tool to characterize criticality in neural systems, validated across models from branching processes to whole-brain models, and shows that FIM of the observed branching ratio peaks near criticality, offering continuous readouts of proximity to criticality without knowing the true control parameter.
AI.motivation: Criticality in neural systems is a topic of deep interest, characterized by power-law avalanches, but empirically estimating critical exponents is challenging and often model-dependent. A comprehensive, model-agnostic characterization of the critical region is needed.
AI.method: The authors demonstrate that the Fisher Information Metric (FIM), a measure of generalized susceptibility, provides a model-agnostic characterization of criticality. They validate this across models of increasing biological complexity (branching processes, spiking models, whole-brain models) by computing FIM of the control parameter. They also compute FIM of the observed branching ratio to emulate real-world scenarios where the control parameter is unknown.
AI.result: FIM of each model's control parameter reliably tracks the degree of criticality. When using the observed branching ratio instead, FIM peaks where activity growth and decay balance, with the peak sharpening as the system approaches criticality. Peak width and height provide continuous, model-free readouts of proximity to criticality.
AI.conclusion: FIM peak width and height yield robust, model-free tools for probing criticality in neural systems without requiring knowledge of the true control parameter, offering a comprehensive solution to the challenge of empirically characterizing criticality.

title: Fisher-Rao Distance Detects Shifts in Kinematic Profiles under Cognitive Load
summary: Motor control research involves the study of movement kinematics derived from the positional trajectories that complex motions describe. In natural, unconstrained motions requiring cognitive and memory processes in real time, the temporal speed profiles are not bell-shaped, may have multiple maxima and the peaks distribution is best fit by the continuous gamma family with two parameters, the shape and the scale. As the stochastic processes described by complex motion trajectories are non-stationary, the gamma shape and scale parameters describing them span stochastic trajectories. These points live on a curved surface where Euclidean distance depends on the arbitrary choice of parameterization. We adopt the Fisher-Rao distance (the geodesic length on the gamma manifold) as a coordinate-free metric for movement fluctuation signatures and present a robust numerical solver that converges across the full range of empirically observed parameters. We demonstrate the metric on a tablet-based digitized Trail Making Test in healthy adults, comparing micromovement fluctuations under low and high cognitive load. Load displaced every participant's fluctuation signature but with no shared direction. Instead, participants converged toward a common operating regime, with those farthest from it at baseline moving the most. Cognitive load thus contracts individuality in motor fluctuations rather than shifting the population uniformly.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a coordinate-free metric based on the Fisher-Rao distance on the gamma manifold to analyze motor control fluctuations, and applies it to tablet-based Trail Making Test data, showing that cognitive load contracts individual differences in motor fluctuations rather than shifting the population uniformly.
AI.motivation: Complex, natural motions produce non-stationary temporal speed profiles that deviate from bell-shaped distributions and are better characterized by the gamma family. The two gamma parameters describing these trajectories span a curved surface where Euclidean distance is parameterization-dependent, so a coordinate-free metric is needed for principled comparison of movement fluctuation signatures.
AI.method: The authors adopt the Fisher-Rao distance (geodesic length on the gamma manifold) as a coordinate-free metric for movement fluctuations, and develop a robust numerical solver that converges across the full range of empirically observed parameter values. They apply this metric to tablet-based digitized Trail Making Test data from healthy adults, comparing micromovement fluctuations under low versus high cognitive load.
AI.result: Cognitive load displaced every participant's fluctuation signature, but the displacement was not in a shared direction. Instead, participants converged toward a common operating regime, with those farthest from that regime at baseline moving the most. Cognitive load contracts individuality in motor fluctuations rather than shifting the population uniformly.
AI.conclusion: The Fisher-Rao distance on the gamma manifold provides a valid, parameterization-free framework for quantifying movement fluctuation differences, and reveals that cognitive load reduces individual differences in motor control signatures rather than producing a uniform population-level shift.

title: MI-PEFT: Mixture-of-Experts Integrated Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning Protein Language Models Improves Acidophilic Proteins Classification
summary: Acidophilic proteins that remain stable and functional under highly acidic conditions, are important for industrial biocatalysis, acid-related bioprocessing, and the discovery of acid-stable enzymes. However, their identification relies heavily on time-consuming experimental screening methods. With the rapid growth of protein sequence databases, the need for computational identification methods that are both accurate and efficient has become stronger. The emergence of protein language models (PLMs) has significantly improved the sequence representation of downstream biological prediction tasks. This paper proposes MI-PEFT, a mixture-of-experts integrated parameter-efficient fine-tuning framework. Built on the ESM C-600M backbone, the framework incorporates LoRA-based PEFT methods and a DeepSeekMoE-based classification head to resolve the limitations of PEFT and significantly improve computational efficiency. Notably, this task is characterized by a significant class imbalance in the dataset, making high specificity particularly challenging. The experimental results demonstrate that MI-PEFT on PLMs, especially {\text{C}}^{\text{3}}\text{A}, serves as an efficient tool for identifying acidophilic proteins and a constrained pathway that helps resolve class-imbalance by preserving the pretrained representations.

AI.tldr: MI-PEFT is a mixture-of-experts integrated parameter-efficient fine-tuning framework built on the ESM C-600M backbone that combines LoRA-based PEFT methods with a DeepSeekMoE-based classification head to computationally identify acidophilic proteins, addressing class imbalance and computational efficiency challenges.
AI.motivation: Acidophilic protein identification relies on time-consuming experimental screening. With rapidly growing protein sequence databases, there is a strong need for accurate and efficient computational identification methods.
AI.method: The paper proposes MI-PEFT, a mixture-of-experts integrated parameter-efficient fine-tuning framework built on the ESM C-600M protein language model backbone. It incorporates LoRA-based PEFT methods and a DeepSeekMoE-based classification head to resolve PEFT limitations and improve computational efficiency, particularly handling the significant class imbalance in the dataset.
AI.result: MI-PEFT on protein language models, especially C3A, serves as an efficient tool for identifying acidophilic proteins and provides a constrained pathway that helps resolve class-imbalance by preserving pretrained representations.
