AI.conclusion: MI-PEFT demonstrates that the proposed MoE-integrated PEFT framework is an efficient computational approach for acidophilic protein identification, effectively addressing both class imbalance and computational efficiency challenges while preserving pretrained representations.

title: PocketVE: Stable and Property-Guided Structure-Based Drug Design with Variance-Exploding Diffusion
summary: Protein-conditioned 3D molecule generation is a central challenge in structure-based drug design, requiring a balance between pocket compatibility, molecular properties, and physical geometry. We propose \textbf{PocketVE}, a protein-pocket-conditioned variance-exploding (VE) diffusion framework that couples stable coordinate denoising with inference-time property guidance. Specifically, PocketVE combines an EDM-style training and sampling setup for 3D denoising, classifier-free guidance for multi-property steering without external property classifiers, and adaptive protein perturbation as a training-time pocket regularizer. Evaluated on CrossDocked2020 under the GenBench3D protocol, PocketVE improves Valid$_{3\text{D}}$ from 58.6 to 80.6 and reduces strain energy from 457.4 to 127.9 relative to its TAGMol architectural baseline, while retaining competitive docking and molecular-property scores under moderate guidance. A guidance-scale study shows that moderate guidance gives a favorable balance between target-related objectives and geometric quality, whereas stronger guidance can degrade geometry and distributional fidelity. Pocket-permutation and PoseCheck diagnostics further support pocket-specific spatial compatibility with reduced steric conflicts. Overall, the results suggest that geometric stability and inference-time property guidance should be considered as coupled design objectives.

AI.tldr: PocketVE is a protein-pocket-conditioned variance-exploding diffusion framework for 3D molecule generation that couples stable coordinate denoising with inference-time property guidance, improving Valid3D from 58.6 to 80.6 and reducing strain energy from 457.4 to 127.9 on CrossDocked2020 under GenBench3D.
AI.motivation: Protein-conditioned 3D molecule generation requires balancing pocket compatibility, molecular properties, and physical geometry—a central challenge in structure-based drug design where existing methods struggle to maintain geometric stability while steering molecular properties.
AI.method: PocketVE combines three key components: (1) an EDM-style training and sampling setup for 3D coordinate denoising with variance-exploding diffusion, (2) classifier-free guidance for multi-property steering without requiring external property classifiers, and (3) adaptive protein perturbation as a training-time pocket regularizer.
AI.result: On CrossDocked2020 under the GenBench3D protocol, PocketVE improves Valid3D from 58.6 to 80.6 and reduces strain energy from 457.4 to 127.9 relative to its TAGMol baseline, while retaining competitive docking and molecular-property scores under moderate guidance. Guidance-scale studies show moderate guidance balances objectives and geometry, while stronger guidance degrades quality.
AI.conclusion: Geometric stability and inference-time property guidance should be considered as coupled design objectives in pocket-conditioned molecule generation, as demonstrated by PocketVE's ability to maintain pocket-specific spatial compatibility with reduced steric conflicts while achieving improved validity and lower strain energy.

title: A Transformer-Based Delta Expression Encoder for Psilocybin Transcriptional Response: Architecture, Representations, and Biological Validation
summary: Understanding why individuals respond differently to psilocybin requires modeling the drug's transcriptional perturbation signature at the cell-type level. I present a Transformer-based delta expression encoder that learns to classify differential gene expression status - upregulated, downregulated, or neutral - from single-nucleus RNA-sequencing data, without supervision from pathway annotations or prior biological knowledge. The model is trained on pseudobulk profiles from 623 examples spanning 18 cell types, 2 drug conditions, and 6 timepoints derived from the Liao et al. 2025 dataset, and achieves 69.4% weighted classification accuracy. Three principal findings are reported, alongside one direct test of a published hypothesis that returned a result inconsistent with that hypothesis. First, per-cell-type classification accuracy ranges from 28.3% (L2/3 IT, a primary HTR2A-expressing psilocybin target) to 99.6% (endothelial cells), consistent with known psilocybin response biology. Second, psilocybin-induced transcriptional downregulation is significantly more stereotyped across individuals than upregulation (Mann-Whitney U=18615.0, p<0.0001), a novel finding with a cortical depth gradient across excitatory subtypes. Third, attention-guided gene co-regulation analysis recovers drug-specific modules without pathway supervision. Separately, a direct test of whether baseline HTR2A expression predicts drug-response separability across cell types found a significant negative correlation (Spearman r = -0.7088, p = 0.0021), the opposite of what a simple HTR2A-gating account would predict.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a Transformer-based delta expression encoder that classifies psilocybin-induced differential gene expression (up/down/neutral) from single-nucleus RNA-seq data without pathway supervision, achieving 69.4% accuracy across 623 pseudobulk examples spanning 18 cell types, 2 drug conditions, and 6 timepoints. Key findings include cell-type-dependent classification accuracy, more stereotyped downregulation than upregulation across individuals, and attention-guided recovery of drug-specific gene modules. A direct test of the HTR2A-gating hypothesis found a significant negative correlation (r=-0.71), contradicting that hypothesis.
AI.motivation: Individual variability in response to psilocybin remains poorly understood, and modeling the drug's transcriptional perturbation at the cell-type level requires a framework that captures differential gene expression without relying on pre-existing biological annotations or pathway knowledge.
AI.method: A Transformer-based delta expression encoder is trained on pseudobulk single-nucleus RNA-seq profiles to classify genes as upregulated, downregulated, or neutral. The model uses attention mechanisms for gene co-regulation analysis and is evaluated on data from the Liao et al. 2025 dataset across multiple cell types, drug conditions, and timepoints.
AI.result: The model achieves 69.4% weighted classification accuracy. Classification accuracy varies widely by cell type (28.3% in L2/3 IT to 99.6% in endothelial cells). Psilocybin-induced downregulation is significantly more stereotyped across individuals than upregulation (Mann-Whitney U=18615.0, p<0.0001), with a cortical depth gradient in excitatory subtypes. Attention-guided analysis recovers drug-specific modules without supervision. A test of HTR2A-gating found a significant negative correlation between baseline HTR2A expression and response separability (Spearman r=-0.7088, p=0.0021), contradicting the expected hypothesis.
AI.conclusion: The Transformer-based approach reveals cell-type-specific psilocybin transcriptional responses and novel asymmetries in downregulation stereotypy. The findings challenge the simple HTR2A-gating account of psilocybin response, suggesting more complex mechanisms govern cell-type variability in drug sensitivity.

title: Predicting directional flexibility in proteins
summary: Predicting protein dynamics is a long-standing problem in computational structural biology. Often, protein function critically depends on local directed motions, such as hinge movements, catalytic loop rearrangements and domain reorientations, which can be characterized by directional flexibility and correlated structural motions of the protein backbone. While Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations provide an established but often prohibitively expensive approach, recent deep generative models aim to reduce this cost by directly predicting conformational ensembles, emulating MD. However, due to their large size and the need to generate several states until the derived dynamical properties converge, these models remain expensive. In this work, we propose BackFlip-2: a fast SE(3)-equivariant graph neural network trained to directly predict dynamical descriptors, such as directional backbone flexibility and pairwise dynamic correlations, from an equilibrium structure. In a series of experiments, we show that our model matches the accuracy of substantially larger ensemble generation models while being orders of magnitude faster, and demonstrate that the proposed equivariant architecture is especially well-suited for capturing anisotropic motions in proteins. BackFlip-2 model weights, training and inference code are available at https://github.com/graeter-group/backflip.

AI.tldr: BackFlip-2 is a fast SE(3)-equivariant graph neural network that directly predicts protein dynamical descriptors (directional backbone flexibility and pairwise dynamic correlations) from an equilibrium structure, matching the accuracy of much larger conformational ensemble generation models while being orders of magnitude faster.
AI.motivation: Predicting protein dynamics is critical for understanding function but Molecular Dynamics simulations are prohibitively expensive. Recent deep generative models predict conformational ensembles to emulate MD, yet these remain expensive due to their large size and the need to generate many states until dynamical properties converge. Thus, there is a need for a faster approach that directly predicts dynamical descriptors.
AI.method: BackFlip-2 uses a fast SE(3)-equivariant graph neural network trained to directly predict dynamical descriptors—specifically directional backbone flexibility and pairwise dynamic correlations—from a single equilibrium protein structure, bypassing the need for ensemble generation.
AI.result: The model matches the accuracy of substantially larger ensemble generation models while being orders of magnitude faster. The equivariant architecture is shown to be especially well-suited for capturing anisotropic motions in proteins.
AI.conclusion: The SE(3)-equivariant GNN approach enables rapid, accurate prediction of directional protein flexibility and correlated motions, offering an efficient alternative to expensive MD simulations and large generative ensemble models.

title: An Evidence-Aware Framework for EEG Microstate Analysis: Improved Sensitivity to Alzheimer's Disease and Ageing
summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) microstate analysis commonly converts each scalp topography into a winner-take-all hard label and summarises the resulting sequence using duration, occurrence, coverage, transitions, and symbolic complexity. Although interpretable, this readout discards evidence strength, assignment ambiguity, and low-confidence periods. We introduce a template evidence trajectory framework that retains, at each sampled Global Field Power (GFP) peak, the evidence for all templates or subject-specific topographic communities. Conventional hard labels are treated as a compressed readout of this multivariate trajectory. We derive two evidence-aware extensions of classical descriptors: high-evidence episode duration and episode rate, which quantify temporal clustering and fragmentation of strong state evidence, and null-state Lempel-Ziv complexity (LZC), which explicitly encodes insufficient-evidence periods. We evaluated the framework across four resting-state EEG datasets spanning Alzheimer's disease and age-related variation. Fixed-state models included K-means, AAHC, and HMMs at K = 4 and K = 7, together with adaptive subject-specific Leiden and Infomap communities. Across 32 dataset-model cases, trajectory-derived duration effects exceeded matched hard-label effects in all cases at the representative setting and in 30-32 cases across a broader parameter grid. Null-state LZC improved over traditional LZC in most cases, while classification showed modest but consistent gains for trajectory or combined features. Retaining template evidence therefore provides a more sensitive readout of EEG topographic state dynamics while remaining compatible with conventional microstate analysis.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a template evidence trajectory framework for EEG microstate analysis that retains continuous evidence for all templates at each GFP peak, rather than discarding it via winner-take-all hard labeling. This enables evidence-aware extensions of classical descriptors (high-evidence episode duration/rate and null-state LZC) that outperform traditional hard-label metrics across 32 dataset-model cases spanning Alzheimer's disease and aging datasets.
AI.motivation: Traditional EEG microstate analysis converts scalp topographies into winner-take-all hard labels, which discards critical information about evidence strength, assignment ambiguity, and low-confidence periods. While interpretable, this compressed readout loses sensitivity to the underlying dynamics of brain states.
AI.method: The framework retains, at each sampled GFP peak, evidence for all templates or subject-specific topographic communities, treating conventional hard labels as a compressed readout of this multivariate trajectory. They derive two evidence-aware extensions: high-evidence episode duration and episode rate (quantifying temporal clustering/fragmentation of strong state evidence) and null-state Lempel-Ziv complexity (encoding insufficient-evidence periods). Evaluated with fixed-state models (K-means, AAHC, HMMs at K=4 and K=7) and adaptive subject-specific communities (Leiden, Infomap) across four resting-state EEG datasets.
AI.result: Across 32 dataset-model cases, trajectory-derived duration effects exceeded matched hard-label effects in all cases at the representative setting and in 30-32 cases across a broader parameter grid. Null-state LZC improved over traditional LZC in most cases, and classification showed modest but consistent gains for trajectory or combined features.
AI.conclusion: Retaining template evidence provides a more sensitive readout of EEG topographic state dynamics while remaining compatible with conventional microstate analysis workflows, suggesting that evidence-aware descriptors offer a principled enhancement over hard-label-based summaries.

title: Multi-ligand simultaneous docking of Carica papaya leaf phytochemicals, Carpaine and Rutin, reveals multi-mechanism inhibition of cancer proteins BCL-2 and WWP1
comment: \c{opyright} 2025 The Author(s). Published by Elsevier B.V
summary: Cancer remains a major global health concern due to chemotherapy resistance and toxicity from high-dose treatments. To overcome these challenges, new therapeutic strategies targeting key proteins in cancer progression are essential. This study evaluates two phytochemicals, Carpaine (Car) and Rutin (Rut), from Carica papaya leaves, for their potential in enhancing cancer therapy by targeting B-cell lymphoma 2 (BCL-2) and WW domain-containing protein 1 (WWP1) proteins. We assessed their additive, allosteric, and synergistic effects using molecular docking, multi-ligand simultaneous docking (MLSD), molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, and MMPBSA analysis. Car and Rut showed an additive effect on BCL-2 by binding at distinct regions within the same pocket. MLSD revealed an improved binding affinity of -13.13 +/- 0.08 kcal/mol, compared with individual ligands or the commercial inhibitor Venetoclax. For WWP1, Car bound near the H-site and Rut near the Le-site, exhibiting an allosteric effect that increased Car's binding affinity in MLSD to -15.59 +/- 0.39 kcal/mol. Furthermore, Rut combined with bortezomib (Bort) demonstrated a synergistic interaction with WWP1. Binding energies were -7.64 +/- 0.156 kcal/mol for Bort, -10.26 +/- 0.07 kcal/mol for Rut, and -15.59 +/- 0.39 kcal/mol for MLSD, suggesting a more stable complex through synergy. These results suggest Car and Rut, particularly in combination with Bort, as promising candidates against cancer-related proteins BCL-2 and WWP1. Further experimental validation is warranted to explore their therapeutic potential.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates two phytochemicals from Carica papaya leaves—Carpaine (Car) and Rutin (Rut)—as potential cancer therapeutic enhancers targeting BCL-2 and WWP1 proteins. Using molecular docking, MLSD, MD simulations, and MMPBSA, the authors found that Car and Rut act additively on BCL-2 and allosterically on WWP1, with improved binding affinities when co-administered, and Rut combined with bortezomib shows synergistic interaction with WWP1, suggesting these compounds as promising candidates for enhanced cancer therapy pending experimental validation.
AI.motivation: Cancer remains a major global health burden due to chemotherapy resistance and toxicity from high-dose treatments. There is a critical need for new therapeutic strategies targeting key cancer-promoting proteins, and natural phytochemicals offer a promising avenue for safer combination therapies.
AI.method: The study used computational approaches including molecular docking, multi-ligand simultaneous docking (MLSD), molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, and MMPBSA binding free energy analysis to evaluate additive, allosteric, and synergistic effects of Carpaine (Car) and Rutin (Rut) targeting BCL-2 and WWP1 proteins.
AI.result: Car and Rut showed an additive effect on BCL-2 (MLSD binding affinity of -13.13 ± 0.08 kcal/mol, better than Venetoclax). For WWP1, they exhibited an allosteric effect with improved binding (-15.59 ± 0.39 kcal/mol in MLSD). Rut combined with bortezomib showed synergy with WWP1, yielding a more stable complex (-15.59 ± 0.39 kcal/mol) than individual ligands.
AI.conclusion: Car and Rut, particularly in combination with bortezomib, are promising candidates against cancer-related proteins BCL-2 and WWP1, though further experimental validation is needed to explore their therapeutic potential.

title: Hi-M imaging of chromatin architecture in adult Drosophila brain cryosections
summary: Hi-M combines fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), automated microfluidics, sequential imaging, and computational chromatin tracing to measure the three-dimensional organization of selected genomic regions in single cells. This chapter describes a Hi-M workflow adapted for cryosections of adult Drosophila melanogaster brains, enabling chromatin tracing while preserving tissue architecture and cell identity. The protocol covers Oligopaint library design and amplification, fixation, brain dissection, cryoprotection, cryosectioning, sequential RNA-FISH for cell-type identification, sequential DNA-FISH labeling, automated acquisition, and chromatin trace reconstruction. We also provide practical guidance for experimental design, sample preparation, tissue handling, image acquisition, and data analysis, highlighting critical steps that influence tissue integrity, hybridization efficiency, image registration, barcode detection, and chromatin trace reconstruction. The workflow is readily adaptable to different genomic loci and cell types, providing a robust approach for studying 3D genome organization in intact adult tissues.

AI.tldr: This paper describes a Hi-M workflow adapted for cryosections of adult Drosophila melanogaster brains, enabling 3D chromatin tracing while preserving tissue architecture and cell identity through a combination of Oligopaint library design, sequential RNA-FISH for cell-type identification, sequential DNA-FISH labeling, automated image acquisition, and computational chromatin trace reconstruction.
AI.motivation: To enable the study of 3D genome organization in intact adult tissues, preserving both tissue architecture and cell identity, which is challenging for existing chromatin tracing methods.
AI.method: The workflow combines Hi-M technology (FISH, automated microfluidics, sequential imaging, computational chromatin tracing) adapted for brain cryosections, covering Oligopaint library design/amplification, fixation, dissection, cryoprotection, cryosectioning, sequential RNA-FISH for cell typing, sequential DNA-FISH, automated acquisition, and trace reconstruction.
AI.result: A robust and adaptable workflow for 3D genome organization studies in intact adult tissues, applicable to different genomic loci and cell types.
AI.conclusion: The Hi-M cryosection workflow provides a practical approach for chromatin tracing in adult tissues while maintaining tissue context and cell identity, with adaptability to various genomic regions and cell types.

title: Selection Rules for Species Coexistence in a Hierarchical May-Leonard Model
summary: One of the central challenges in evolutionary dynamics is understanding why some species combinations persist while others disappear. Although cyclic-interaction models have provided fundamental insights into biodiversity maintenance, much less is known about how hierarchical competitive interactions shape long-term community organization. Here, we investigate a hierarchical extension of the May-Leonard model, in which species interact through a directed predation chain while undergoing reproduction and mortality. Combining mean-field analysis with Monte Carlo simulations, we show that the fully coexisting state is generically unstable, causing the dynamics to evolve toward lower-dimensional coexistence states. The simulations further reveal stochastic extinctions dominating small populations with the dynamics progressively approaching the mean-field predictions as the system size increases. Rather than permitting arbitrary species combinations, the hierarchical-interaction structure dynamically constrains coexistence by selecting only specific subsets of species for long-term persistence. We show that these admissible coexistence states have a natural graph-theoretic interpretation as independent sets in the hierarchical interaction network, thereby providing general constraints on coexistence in hierarchical communities. Together, these results establish a theoretical framework linking hierarchical interactions, dynamical selection, graph topology, and biodiversity organization, extending the classical May-Leonard model beyond cyclic competition.

AI.tldr: This paper extends the May-Leonard model to hierarchical (predation-chain) competitive interactions, showing through mean-field analysis and Monte Carlo simulations that full coexistence is generically unstable, stochastic extinctions dominate small populations, and only specific species subsets—interpretable as independent sets in the hierarchical interaction network—can persist long-term, linking graph topology to biodiversity organization.
AI.motivation: While cyclic-interaction models have greatly advanced our understanding of biodiversity maintenance, much less is known about how hierarchical competitive interactions shape long-term community organization. The authors aim to fill this gap by extending classical cyclic competition models to hierarchical structures.
AI.method: The authors extend the May-Leonard model to include hierarchical interactions forming a directed predation chain, combined with reproduction and mortality. They use a combination of mean-field analysis and Monte Carlo simulations across varying system sizes.
AI.result: The fully coexisting state is generically unstable, driving dynamics toward lower-dimensional coexistence states. Stochastic extinctions dominate in small populations, while dynamics approach mean-field predictions as system size increases. Only specific subsets of species (admissible coexistence states) can persist, which correspond to independent sets in the hierarchical interaction network.
AI.conclusion: The findings establish a theoretical framework linking hierarchical interactions, dynamical selection, graph topology, and biodiversity organization, thereby extending the classical May-Leonard model beyond cyclic competition and providing general constraints on coexistence in hierarchical communities.

title: Unique steady states for population models in a heterogeneous environment
summary: We revisit a model proposed by Freedman etal in \cite{freedman} which describes the dynamics of a population diffusing in a patchy environment. From their work it is known that positive steady states exist for this model, but not whether they are unique. Here, we provide sufficient conditions guaranteeing that steady states are unique. These conditions are satisfied when the reaction rates are generalized logistic growth rates. Our proofs critically exploit Chicone's ideas in \cite{chicone}, which were used to establish that the period map associated to a continuous family of periodic solutions of certain planar Hamiltonian systems is monotone.

AI.tldr: This paper provides sufficient conditions guaranteeing the uniqueness of positive steady states for a population diffusion model in a patchy environment, originally proposed by Freedman et al. The conditions are satisfied for generalized logistic growth rates, and the proofs exploit Chicone's ideas on monotonicity of period maps in planar Hamiltonian systems.
AI.motivation: While it was previously known that positive steady states exist for the Freedman et al. model of population dynamics in a patchy environment, it was not known whether they are unique. Establishing uniqueness is important for understanding the long-term dynamics and predictability of the system.
AI.method: The authors provide sufficient conditions guaranteeing uniqueness of steady states by critically exploiting Chicone's ideas, originally used to establish monotonicity of the period map associated to continuous families of periodic solutions of certain planar Hamiltonian systems.
AI.result: The sufficient conditions for uniqueness of steady states are satisfied when the reaction rates are generalized logistic growth rates.
AI.conclusion: Positive steady states for the patchy environment diffusion model are unique under generalized logistic growth rates, resolving an open question from Freedman et al.'s work.

title: From the SIR/SEIR/SVEIR Model to a Chemotactic System: Analysis of Spatiotemporal Mechanisms of Infection Spread within the Einstein Paradigm
summary: This work investigates the class of SIR/SEIR models and their extension to an ODE-based SVEIR system, whose parameters are calibrated and validated using real influenza outbreak data. The theoretical part establishes existence and uniqueness of solutions for the SVEIR model via the Picard-Lindelof theorem and analyzes invariance of the admissible region. To describe spatiotemporal infection spread in an urban setting, a diffusion-chemotaxis extension of the SIR framework is formulated as a PDE system; an additional term is introduced to represent fear/avoidance effects in the system dynamics. A numerical workflow is proposed, including grid discretization, Neumann boundary conditions enforced by mirror extension, a semi-implicit IMEX time-stepping scheme, and sparse linear solves; computational correctness is monitored, in particular, by checking conservation of the total population.

AI.tldr: This paper studies SIR/SEIR epidemiological models and an ODE-based SVEIR extension, calibrated with real influenza data. The theory (existence, uniqueness) relies on Picard-Lindelof, while a PDE diffusion-chemotaxis SIR model captures spatiotemporal spread in urban settings with fear/avoidance dynamics. A numeric workflow (IMEX, grid discretization, boundary handling, sparse solvers) ensures computational correctness via population conservation checks.
AI.motivation: To extend classic epidemic compartmental models with vaccination and spatial dynamics, incorporating behavioral effects like fear/avoidance for more realistic urban infection spread prediction.
AI.method: ODE-based SVEIR modeling with theoretical guarantees, extended to a diffusion-chemotaxis PDE system; solved via a structured numerical framework using IMEX time stepping, Neumann boundary mirror extension, and sparse linear algebra with conservation monitoring.
AI.result: Calibrated and validated model parameters using real influenza outbreak data; theoretical and numerical properties (well-posedness, solution invariance, population conservation) are established and verified.
AI.conclusion: The combined SVEIR/ODE-PDE modeling with behavioral terms and robust numerics provides a reliable framework for epidemic forecasting, spatiotemporal analysis, and vaccination strategy assessment in urban environments.

title: A Network-Structured Bayesian Hierarchical Model for Sparse Mutation-Drug Response Associations: Application to Cancer Pharmacogenomics
comment: The manuscript is under review with Biostatistics (Oxford Academic)
summary: We develop a network-structured Bayesian hierarchical model for sparse association mapping between genomic alterations and quantitative treatment-response phenotypes. The framework combines a Gaussian Markov random field prior that borrows strength across pathway-connected genes, a global-local horseshoe prior inducing sparsity, and a conjugate Gibbs sampler requiring no Metropolis-Hastings steps. Though broadly applicable to high-dimensional settings with known predictor networks, we validate it using cancer cell-line drug-sensitivity data. Applied to GDSC2 ($N=951$ cell lines, $G=219$ driver genes, $D=295$ drugs), the model identifies 126 gene-drug associations (0.195\% of 64{,}605 pairs), concentrated in EZH2 (45 drugs, all sensitivity-direction, mean effect $-0.911$ $\ln$IC50) and KMT2D (36 drugs, all sensitivity-direction, mean effect $-0.496$ $\ln$IC50). These markers show external support in an independent PRISM screen (1{,}518 compounds), with KMT2D achieving complete directional replication (36/36) and EZH2 partial replication (8/12). Five-fold cross-validated predictive log-likelihood confirms each prior layer's value: the full model outperforms the no-network ablation by $+3{,}109$ log-units per fold and the no-horseshoe ablation by $+14{,}039$ log-units, consistently across folds. Simulations under three scenarios show the full model achieves the highest precision and lowest false-discovery rate throughout, while the network prior improves sensitivity recovery under network-structured signal. A tissue-stratified extension identifies coherent subgroup refinements, including lung-specific EGFR-inhibitor sensitivity and skin-specific BRAF-Dabrafenib sensitivity. These results show the framework identifies sparse, interpretable, externally supported drug-sensitivity markers while enabling principled investigation of tissue-specific departures from shared effects.

AI.tldr: A Bayesian hierarchical network-structured model combining Gaussian Markov random field and horseshoe priors for sparse association mapping between genomic alterations and drug-sensitivity phenotypes, validated on GDSC2 cancer cell-line data (identifying 126 gene-drug associations) with external replication in PRISM and tissue-stratified extensions.
AI.motivation: To identify sparse, interpretable associations between genomic alterations and treatment-response phenotypes while leveraging known pathway/gene-network structure and accounting for high-dimensional predictor settings—addressing limitations of methods that ignore network connectivity or lack Bayesian uncertainty quantification.
AI.method: A network-structured Bayesian hierarchical model combining: (1) a Gaussian Markov random field (GMRF) prior that borrows strength across pathway-connected genes, (2) a global-local horseshoe prior for sparsity induction, and (3) a conjugate Gibbs sampler requiring no Metropolis-Hastings steps. Includes a tissue-stratified extension for subgroup-specific effects.
AI.result: On GDSC2 (N=951 cell lines, 219 genes, 295 drugs), the model identifies 126 gene-drug associations (0.195% of 64,605 pairs), concentrated in EZH2 (45 drugs) and KMT2D (36 drugs). KMT2D achieves complete directional replication (36/36) in PRISM; EZH2 partial (8/12). Full model outperforms no-network ablation by +3,109 log-units/fold and no-horseshoe ablation by +14,039 log-units. Simulations confirm highest precision/lowest FDR. Tissue-stratified analysis finds EGFR-inhibitor lung sensitivity and BRAF-Dabrafenib skin sensitivity.
AI.conclusion: The framework identifies sparse, interpretable, externally supported drug-sensitivity markers while enabling principled investigation of tissue-specific departures from shared effects, demonstrating the value of both network and sparsity priors in high-dimensional genomic association mapping.

title: Agentic BAIM-LLM Evaluation (ABLE): Benchmarking LLM Use of Protein Design Tools
comment: Last revised in February 2026; presented without further revision. An earlier revision at was presented at the NeurIPS 2025 Workshop on Biosecurity Safeguards for Generative AI; see https://openreview.net/forum?id=fDysOrWaGd
summary: We introduce ABLE, a benchmark for evaluating LLM agents' ability to use biological AI models (BAIMs), such as ProteinMPNN and AlphaFold3, in dual-use protein design workflows. ABLE assesses agent performance through a set of tasks spanning structure retrieval, sequence generation, and design validation. We evaluate 15 frontier models and find that seven refuse all tasks, while the remaining models exhibit substantial performance differences. Claude Sonnet 4 and Gemini 3 Pro achieve the highest scores across information retrieval, tool selection, and tool use. We further compare model performance on a subset of tasks against an expert human baseline. Our results suggest that current LLMs can substantially lower barriers to protein design, but remain inconsistent in planning, strategy generation, and integrating biological knowledge with tool use.

AI.tldr: ABLE is a benchmark evaluating LLM agents' ability to use biological AI models (BAIMs) like ProteinMPNN and AlphaFold3 in dual-use protein design workflows. Fifteen frontier models were tested; seven refused all tasks, while Claude Sonnet 4 and Gemini 3 Pro performed best. Results show LLMs can lower barriers to protein design but remain inconsistent in planning and integrating biological knowledge with tool use.
AI.motivation: To assess whether LLM agents can effectively operate biological AI models in protein design workflows, particularly given the dual-use safety concerns and the need to understand current capabilities and limitations of AI agents in this domain.
AI.method: The authors introduce the ABLE benchmark with tasks spanning structure retrieval, sequence generation, and design validation. They evaluate 15 frontier LLM models on these tasks and compare a subset of model performance against an expert human baseline.
AI.result: Seven of 15 frontier models refused all tasks. Claude Sonnet 4 and Gemini 3 Pro achieved the highest scores across information retrieval, tool selection, and tool use. Models showed substantial performance differences, with current LLMs demonstrating an ability to lower barriers to protein design but exhibiting inconsistency in planning, strategy generation, and integrating biological knowledge with tools.
AI.conclusion: Current LLM agents can meaningfully assist in protein design workflows using biological AI models, but their inconsistency in strategic planning and biological knowledge integration indicates significant room for improvement before they approach expert-level reliability.

title: Fluidization in Growth-Induced Morphogenesis
summary: Elastic buckling has explained shape formation in growing tissues, yet the role of tissue fluidity remains elusive. We derive a minimal fluidized growth-elasticity model as a nonlinear analogue of Maxwell rheology. Analysis of a growing strip shows that fluidity promotes symmetry breaking under compression while regulating stress accumulation, so morphogenesis develops continuously before the elastic buckling threshold. Fluidity further controls the flow pattern, from smooth sinusoidal undulations to widened crests and localized indentations, with low fluidity favoring stronger localization.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a minimal fluidized growth-elasticity model (a nonlinear analogue of Maxwell rheology) showing that tissue fluidity promotes symmetry breaking under compression before the elastic buckling threshold, and controls morphogenesis flow patterns from sinusoidal undulations to localized indentations depending on fluidity levels.
AI.motivation: While elastic buckling has been used to explain shape formation in growing tissues, the role of tissue fluidity—a key mechanical property of biological tissues—remains poorly understood. This gap motivates deriving a framework that accounts for both growth-induced stress and fluid-like relaxation behaviors.
AI.method: The authors derive a minimal fluidized growth-elasticity model, formulated as a nonlinear analogue of Maxwell rheology (combining elastic and viscous/fluid elements). They then perform analysis on a growing strip configuration to examine symmetry breaking and pattern formation under compressive stress.
AI.result: Fluidity promotes symmetry breaking under compression while regulating stress accumulation, enabling continuous morphogenesis before the elastic buckling threshold is reached. Fluidity also controls flow morphology: low fluidity produces smooth sinusoidal undulations, while varying fluidity yields widened crests and localized indentations, with stronger localization favored at low fluidity.
AI.conclusion: Tissue fluidity is a key regulator of morphogenetic pattern formation, allowing shape changes to develop gradually (rather than via sharp buckling transitions) and controlling the spatial character of deformation patterns from smooth waves to localized features.

title: Formation of structural attractors in neuromorphic systems
summary: This paper examines the theory of Invariant Structural Learning (ISL), which proposes a non-optimization approach to concept formation. Learning is interpreted as convergence to structural attractors in a hypergraph space, rather than as the minimization of a global loss function. The paper presents the ISL model, including its mathematical formalization, computational verification, and a hypothetical neurobiological interpretation. The mathematical section introduces the formal apparatus of the structural reduction process and proves its finite convergence, the existence and uniqueness of class structural attractors, and the self-organization of attractor maps. The computational section demonstrates the feasibility of the proposed approach on classical image recognition tasks, utilizing the proposed learning mechanism without backpropagation and with extremely small training datasets. Finally, the neurobiological section formulates hypotheses regarding the possible implementation of structural attractors in dendritic trees, neural coding as a projection of internal attractor dynamics, and the development of neural architectures supporting the proposed learning concept. These hypotheses are discussed in the context of modern experimental data in the fields of dendritic computations, synaptic plasticity, and the structural organization of neural circuits. The proposed neurobiological mechanisms are presented as testable hypotheses rather than established biological facts. The results demonstrate the mathematical consistency and computational feasibility of the proposed model, while the neurobiological hypotheses outline potential directions for its experimental verification.

AI.tldr: This paper presents Invariant Structural Learning (ISL), a non-optimization theory of concept formation where learning is modeled as convergence to structural attractors in a hypergraph space rather than loss minimization. It provides mathematical formalization proving convergence properties, computational validation on image recognition with tiny datasets and no backpropagation, and testable neurobiological hypotheses about dendritic implementations.
AI.motivation: The paper seeks to challenge the dominant optimization-based paradigm of learning (loss function minimization/backpropagation) by proposing an alternative theoretical framework where learning emerges from structural convergence dynamics, potentially addressing limitations of current approaches such as large data requirements and lack of biological plausibility.
AI.method: The ISL model is developed across three domains: (1) Mathematical: a formal structural reduction process is defined, with proofs of finite convergence, existence/uniqueness of class structural attractors, and self-organization of attractor maps; (2) Computational: the mechanism is implemented and tested on classical image recognition tasks without backpropagation using extremely small training datasets; (3) Neurobiological: hypotheses are formulated linking structural attractors to dendritic trees, neural coding as projections of internal attractor dynamics, and neural architecture development, framed as testable hypotheses contextualized with modern experimental data.
AI.result: The paper demonstrates mathematical consistency (finite convergence, attractor existence/uniqueness, self-organization) and computational feasibility of ISL on classical image recognition tasks, achieving results with extremely small training datasets and no backpropagation. The neurobiological hypotheses are presented as testable propositions rather than established facts.
AI.conclusion: ISL provides a mathematically consistent and computationally feasible alternative to optimization-based learning. The neurobiological hypotheses outline concrete directions for experimental verification, positioning the framework as a testable theory rather than a complete biological account.

title: MedGSSR: Generalizable Medical Image Super-Resolution 3D Reconstruction via Hierarchical Feed-forward Gaussian Splatting
summary: High-resolution volumetric medical imaging is critical for clinical diagnosis, yet acquisition is often limited by scanner hardware, scan time, and for CT, radiation dose. Medical 3D Super-Resolution (Med3DSR) offers a computational alternative, but existing methods commonly rely on per-subject optimization, pretrained priors, or coordinate-based implicit representations, which compromise anatomical fidelity and limit efficiency. To address these limitations, we present MedGSSR, a fully end-to-end feed-forward framework that represents volumes as an explicit 3D Gaussian field for Med3DSR. Unlike coordinate-based implicit functions, our explicit 3D Gaussian representation naturally enhances signal continuity and local high-frequency fidelity. Specifically, MedGSSR explicitly decouples the reconstruction process into coarse-grained structural preservation and fine-grained textural refinement through the proposed Pyramid Anatomical Encoder and a Hierarchical Gaussian Projector. To support arbitrary-scale super-resolution, we introduce sub-voxel Gaussian decomposition and a Differentiable Gaussian Voxelizer that directly queries the continuous 3D intensity field, reducing discretization artifacts. Extensive experiments on MRI and CT benchmarks demonstrate that MedGSSR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Notably, our framework exhibits robust generalizability across unseen datasets without requiring per-subject optimization, enabling fast inference and high-fidelity volumetric super-resolution in practical clinical settings. Our project webpage, including code, is at https://william2ai.github.io/medgssr

Existing Med3DSR methods rely on per-subject optimization, pretrained priors, or coordinate-based implicit representations, which compromise anatomical fidelity and limit efficiency.

title: Attributing Cohen's d: Training Data Attribution for Disease-Related Effects in Normative Age Biomarkers
summary: Normative age models are trained to predict chronological age in a nominally healthy cohort. Applied to patients, they deviate, and the gap between predicted and chronological age is read as disease risk. Here, we attribute the disease-related effect size of the age gap directly to individual training samples, rather than using a prediction-level loss as the attribution target. For Cohen's $d$, the resulting closed-form influence functional, validated against leave-one-out retraining, ranks training samples by their effect on held-out case-control separation. Across four diseases and two biomarker modalities in UK Biobank, removing the 10% most influential training samples raises held-out disease-related effect size in every seed. It more than doubles the metabolomic-age effect for type-2 diabetes and raises the brain-age effect for multiple sclerosis by roughly a third. Random removal leaves effect size flat even at 50% removal, confirming the gain comes from which samples are removed, not how many. Flagged subjects carry subclinical cardiometabolic burden that diagnosis-based exclusion misses, on markers the model never sees. For type-2 diabetes, where the method gains most, the marker recovered is HbA1c, the standard measure of blood sugar control. We release pyinfluence, our influence-function package, for reproducibility and reuse.

Across four diseases and two biomarker modalities in UK Biobank, removing the most influential 10% of training samples boosts held-out disease-related effect size in every seed (more than doubling the metabolomic-age effect for type-2 diabetes and raising brain-age effect for multiple sclerosis by ~1/3), while random removal has no effect. Flagged samples carry subclinical disease burden missed by diagnosis-based exclusion, and the method is released as the pyinfluence package.
AI.motivation: Normative age models predict chronological age in healthy cohorts and interpret the gap between predicted and chronological age (the "age gap") as disease risk in patients. However, existing approaches typically measure this effect at the prediction level, leaving an open question of which individual training samples drive the disease-related effect size of the age gap—information that could improve model training and reveal disease-relevant markers.

This is validated against leave-one-out retraining and used to rank training samples by their influence on held-out case-control separation.
AI.result: Across four diseases and two biomarker modalities in UK Biobank, removing the 10% most influential training samples raises held-out disease-related effect size in every seed. The metabolomic-age effect for type-2 diabetes more than doubles, and brain-age effect for multiple sclerosis rises by roughly a third. Random removal leaves effect size flat even at 50% removal. Flagged subjects carry subclinical cardiometabolic burden on markers the model never sees (e.g., HbA1c, the standard blood-sugar-control measure, recovered for type-2 diabetes).
AI.conclusion: Selectively identifying and removing influential training samples can substantially enhance the disease-discriminative power of normative age models, with gains attributable to which samples are removed rather than how many. The released pyinfluence package enables reproducibility and broader reuse.

title: The Accuracy Paradox: Empirical Diagnostic of Default Decision Thresholds in Multi-Label Enzyme Commission Prediction [With Code]

summary: Automated prediction of Enzyme Commission (EC) numbers plays a central role in functional annotation and computational drug discovery. However, standard multi-label machine learning pipelines frequently rely on default decision thresholds (t=0.50), assuming balanced prior distributions across target heads. In this study, we present a systematic empirical diagnostic of uncalibrated fixed decision boundaries operating under severe class imbalance across N = 14,096 annotated compounds categorized into six primary EC classes (EC1-EC6). Our results highlight a pronounced Accuracy Paradox: while the multi-label system achieves a deceivingly high mean accuracy of 77.16%, the macro F1-score (0.3976) and macro recall (0.3872) reveal severe predictive breakdown. Majority target classes suffer from hyper-sensitivity and over-prediction, whereas minority classes exhibit sharp recall decay, culminating in a total decision boundary collapse for EC6 (Recall = 0.00%) despite underlying discriminative power (ROC-AUC = 0.5857). Feature correlation analysis further reveals high linear redundancy among topological indices relative to fingerprint density metrics. Ultimately, this diagnostic study demonstrates that standard point predictions mask critical errors in bioinformatics workflows. We establish target-specific threshold optimization and post-hoc conformal calibration as essential, open-source post-processing safeguards for reliable applied machine learning and deep learning architectures.

title: Completion of DNA replication is constrained by the spatiotemporal organisation of origin firing
summary: DNA replication requires the coordination of origin firing and fork progression to ensure the entire genome is timely duplicated before cell division. Yet origin firing is stochastic, giving rise to the classical random completion problem of how probabilistic local events can nevertheless ensure reliable genome duplication. Although several biological mechanisms have been proposed to resolve this problem, a quantitative account of how heterogeneous initiation and fork speed govern the persistence of the final unreplicated regions is still lacking. To address this gap, we introduce a population-level kinetic framework that extends KJMA nucleation-and-growth models by tracking unreplicated intervals over size, genomic position and time. We establish well-posedness of the resulting mean-field system and global existence for compatible data. Notably, by introducing a local initiation mass function, we quantify how the density and spatial organisation of origin firing constrain replication completion, yielding novel and sharp upper bounds on both the worst-locus unreplicated fraction and locuswise near-completion time. These results provide a rigorous and computable foundation for mapping vulnerabilities in replication completion and relating persistent unreplicated regions to replication stress and genome instability.

It establishes well-posedness of the mean-field system and derives sharp upper bounds on worst-locus unreplicated fraction and near-completion time using a local initiation mass function, providing a rigorous foundation for understanding replication stress and genome instability.

AI.method: The authors develop a population-level kinetic framework extending KJMA (Kolmogorov-Johnson-Mehl-Avrami) nucleation-and-growth models by tracking unreplicated intervals over size, genomic position and time. They introduce a local initiation mass function and derive mean-field systems with proven well-posedness and global existence for compatible data.

title: A Gradient-based yet Spike-Timing-Dependent Solution to the Feedback Learning Problem in Neural Microcircuits
summary: The brain uses discrete spikes for dynamic computation, yet, how neural microcircuits (NMCs) solve temporal credit assignment using local spike timing remains a fundamental open question. Dominant spiking neural network (SNN) approaches circumvent this by approximating backpropagation through surrogate gradients, decoupling learning from biological spike timing. Here, we reformulate temporal credit assignment as a state separation problem: extracting task-required components induced by historical perturbations directly from the current neural state. This enables an online feedback learning framework for NMCs through a gradient tunneling (GT) algorithm and the lead-lag expansion technique that derives credit assignment from local synaptic spike timing, while remaining compatible with ANN-SNN hybrid architectures. Experimentally, GT-trained NMCs excel at long-timescale evidence integration and noise-robust memory retention, and perform comparably to leading SNN online learning methods on real-world benchmarks with far fewer parameters. The proposed framework addresses the two-decade-old NMC feedback learning problem and suggests a computationally plausible explanation for the brain's learning mechanisms.

GT-trained NMCs perform comparably to leading SNN online learning methods on real-world benchmarks with far fewer parameters.

title: Development, Evaluation, and Multicenter Clinical-Trial Application of an Artificial Intelligence-Assisted MRI Method for Quantitative Knee Cartilage Morphometry
summary: Objective: To develop and evaluate an AI-assisted MRI method for quantitative knee cartilage morphometry in a multicenter phase III knee osteoarthritis trial. Methods: AI pre-segmentation used 3D full-resolution nnU-Net. Version 1.0 used separate femorotibial- and patellar-cartilage models, whereas version 2.0 used a unified three-class model trained on gold-standard annotations. Trial images then underwent two-reader correction and third-reader adjudication. Adjudicated masks were partitioned into medial/lateral femoral and tibial cartilage plus patellar cartilage. Cartilage volume was measured in physical coordinates, mean thickness by 3D ray tracing (3D-RT), and surface area with local thickness <1.5 mm by a 3D ray-based area method (3D-RBA). Evaluation included 1,189 phase III MRI examinations, reader agreement, 20 synthetic thinning models, and a 69-participant longitudinal comparison with 3D-PMA and three comparator thickness methods. Results: Overall pre-segmentation Dice was 0.964 +/- 0.030 (median 0.970), with 78.7% achieving Dice >=0.95. Inter-reader ICCs for cartilage volume were 0.959-0.995. In the 69-participant subset, total cartilage volume increased from 14,184.366 mm^3 at V0 to 15,359.345 mm^3 at V8; 3D-RBA and 3D-PMA decreased by 4.70% and 6.88%, and all four thickness measures were highest at V8. In 20 geometric experiments, MAPE was 5.73%, CCC 0.822, and Dice 0.956. The workflow was applied to 1,188 MRI examinations from 416 participants. From V0 to V8, the treatment group showed +3.45% total cartilage volume, +2.46% mean thickness, and -4.54% 3D-RBA, versus -2.08%, -1.32%, and +0.16% in controls. Conclusion: This workflow provided a reproducible MRI cartilage assessment framework for a multicenter KOA trial. Cross-method agreement and geometric validation supported 3D-RT and 3D-RBA for therapeutic efficacy evaluation.

Cartilage volume was measured in physical coordinates, mean thickness by 3D ray tracing (3D-RT), and low-thickness surface area by 3D ray-based area (3D-RBA). Validation included 1,189 MRI exams, reader agreement, 20 synthetic thinning models, and longitudinal comparison with 3D-PMA and three comparator thickness methods.

title: Fixed-Dimensional Latent Flow for Generating Variable-Size 3D Molecules
summary: In molecular discovery, molecule size is coupled to composition, structure, and other target properties. Yet most 3D generators require molecule size to be specified before generation. Here, we introduce Equivariant-Free Transformer-Autoencoded Latent Flow Matching, a two-stage generative framework that relies entirely on a single fixed-dimensional molecule-level latent representation to generate variable-size molecules. The second-stage flow matching model samples this latent vector, and an autoregressive Transformer decoder then determines molecule size while generating atom types, coordinates, and chemically informative states. Canonical atom ordering and rigid-pose alignment enable standard Transformers without equivariant layers, while joint decoding of molecular geometry and an enriched chemical state enables reliable, deterministic, chemistry-guided graph recovery without requiring a learned dense pairwise bond decoder. The same fixed-dimensional latent supports unconditional and property-conditioned flow matching, while optional property supervision adds an internal ranking readout, with no separate predictor or reference calculations. On PCQM4Mv2, EF-TALFM achieves the highest fraction of molecules that are unique, training-set novel, pass sanitization and PoseBusters sanity checks, 89.4\%, compared with 75.6\% for UAE-3D and 69.8\% for FlowMol. EF-TALFM also achieves higher measured computational throughput for training and sampling. Across ten target HOMO--LUMO gaps, internal ranking doubles the density functional theory (DFT)-verified hit rate within $0.1\,\mathrm{eV}$, while preserving 97\% novelty among unique verified hits. These results demonstrate that fixed-dimensional molecule-level generation followed by symmetry-resolved autoregressive realization provides a practical architecture for open-ended and property-directed 3D molecular design.

AI.tldr: EF-TALFM is a two-stage generative framework for 3D molecular design that uses a single fixed-dimensional molecule-level latent representation to generate variable-size molecules. It combines flow matching for latent sampling with an autoregressive Transformer decoder for molecule realization, achieving state-of-the-art validity (89.4% vs 75.6% UAE-3D and 69.8% FlowMol on PCQM4Mv2) with higher computational throughput.
AI.motivation: Most 3D molecular generators require molecule size to be specified beforehand, but size is naturally coupled to composition and structure in molecular discovery. This creates an artificial constraint limiting open-ended generation.
AI.method: Two-stage framework: (1) A fixed-dimensional molecule-level latent representation is sampled via flow matching (supporting both unconditional and property-conditioned generation); (2) An autoregressive Transformer decoder generates variable-size molecules by jointly decoding atom types, coordinates, and chemically informative states. Canonical atom ordering and rigid-pose alignment allow standard transformers without equivariant layers. Joint decoding of geometry and chemical state enables deterministic chemistry-guided graph recovery without a learned dense pairwise bond decoder. Optional property supervision adds an internal ranking readout without separate predictors.
AI.result: On PCQM4Mv2, EF-TALFM achieves 89.4% valid unique novel molecules (highest fraction passing sanitization and PoseBusters checks), versus 75.6% for UAE-3D and 69.8% for FlowMol. It also achieves higher measured computational throughput for both training and sampling. Across ten target HOMO-LUMO gaps, internal ranking doubles the DFT-verified hit rate within 0.1 eV while preserving 97% novelty among unique verified hits.
AI.conclusion: Fixed-dimensional molecule-level generation followed by symmetry-resolved autoregressive realization provides a practical and effective architecture for both open-ended and property-directed 3D molecular design, eliminating the need for pre-specifying molecule size.

title: Why shared attention vectors fail: a case for outcome-indexed tuning
summary: Dimensional attention in learning is often implemented as a globally shared attention vector, where each stimulus dimension corresponds to a single scalar. These scalars are learned by models through gradient-descent on error, where predictive features acquire more salience. We show that under multi-outcome learning, where models predict more than one outcome, this shared vector becomes unstable; it collapses to its bounds and prevents the models from learning meaningful attentional tunings for learning and generalization. We address this by introducing an outcome-indexed attentional matrix that converts globally shared attentional tuning into an outcome-indexed representation. We present an analysis of the unstable shared vectors and derive the conditions under which it holds. Empirically, three synthetic experiments benchmark the proposed attention matrices and show that they converge to meaningful representations, something shared attention vectors fail to do. These results suggest that outcome-indexed attentional matrices are a general fix for gradient-based attentional processes, which improves models of learning under multi-outcome conditions.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies a failure mode in gradient-based dimensional attention learning under multi-outcome conditions: globally shared attention vectors become unstable and collapse to their bounds, preventing meaningful learning. The authors propose an outcome-indexed attentional matrix as a fix and demonstrate empirically that it converges to meaningful representations while shared vectors fail.
AI.motivation: Dimensional attention in learning models is typically implemented as a globally shared attention vector where each stimulus dimension maps to a single scalar. Under multi-outcome learning (predicting more than one outcome), this shared vector becomes unstable, collapses to its bounds, and prevents models from learning meaningful attentional tunings needed for learning and generalization. The paper aims to diagnose this instability and address it.
AI.method: The authors introduce an outcome-indexed attentional matrix that replaces the globally shared attentional tuning with an outcome-indexed representation. They provide a theoretical analysis of the unstable shared vectors and derive the conditions under which this instability holds. They then benchmark the proposed attention matrices against shared attention vectors in three synthetic experiments.
AI.result: The three synthetic experiments show that outcome-indexed attentional matrices converge to meaningful representations, whereas shared attention vectors fail to do so under multi-outcome conditions.
AI.conclusion: Outcome-indexed attentional matrices serve as a general fix for gradient-based attentional processes, improving models of learning under multi-outcome conditions where shared attention vectors are unstable.

title: Speed and stability of segregated waves in a pressure-based model of heterogeneous cell populations
summary: We consider a minimal pressure-based model of heterogeneous cell populations consisting of proliferative and non-proliferative cells with different mobilities. The model is formulated as a system of reaction--cross--diffusion equations describing the spatio-temporal dynamics of the cell densities. The model is known to admit one-dimensional travelling wave solutions with strictly segregated components: non-proliferative cells occupy a finite region at the leading edge, while proliferative cells remain at the rear. However, the speed, parameter dependence, and stability of these waves remain poorly understood. In this work, we derive an almost explicit variational bound on the wave speed by reformulating the problem as a free-boundary problem for a generalised porous--Fisher equation. The estimates we obtain apply to general pressure laws and growth kinetics, agree closely with the results of numerical simulations, and become sharp in the incompressible limit, where we formally recover a fully explicit characterisation of the wave speed. We then analyse the stability of the waves to show that segregated waves are stable only when non-proliferative cells are more mobile than proliferative cells. Finally, motivated by numerical observations of finger-like protrusions, we investigate the stability of incompressible segregated circular waves through asymptotic shape-perturbation analysis. This yields explicit expressions for the pressure, interface velocity, and growth rates of angular modes, thereby making evident the destabilisation mechanisms that may lead to the emergence of fingering instability. Interestingly, we find that, in contrast with the one-dimensional case, the stability of such circular waves is not determined solely by the relative value of the mobility coefficients, and thus instabilities may arise irrespective of which cell type has the larger mobility.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes a two-phase (proliferative/non-proliferative) pressure-based model of heterogeneous cell populations, deriving almost explicit variational bounds on traveling wave speeds via a free-boundary reformulation, proving that segregated planar waves are stable only when non-proliferative cells are more mobile, and using asymptotic shape-perturbation analysis to show that circular incompressible waves can be unstable regardless of relative mobility, unlike the 1D case.
AI.motivation: The model admits one-dimensional traveling wave solutions with strictly segregated cell populations, but the speed, parameter dependence, and stability of these waves were poorly understood. Understanding these aspects is important for predicting and controlling tissue growth dynamics.
AI.method: The paper reformulates the reaction-cross-diffusion system as a free-boundary problem for a generalized porous-Fisher equation, derives an almost explicit variational bound on wave speed, performs linear stability analysis for planar segregated waves, and employs asymptotic shape-perturbation analysis for incompressible circular waves.
AI.result: Variational bounds on wave speed apply to general pressure laws and growth kinetics, agree well with numerics, and become sharp (fully explicit) in the incompressible limit. Planar segregated waves are stable only when non-proliferative cells are more mobile. Circular wave stability is NOT determined solely by relative mobility—instabilities can arise irrespective of which cell type is more mobile.
AI.conclusion: The findings reveal a striking contrast between 1D planar and 2D circular segregated waves: while planar stability depends only on mobility ordering, circular waves can exhibit fingering instabilities regardless of which cell type has higher mobility, suggesting richer destabilization mechanisms in radial geometries.
